utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Justice Jackson concluded that: "... our profession should see that it is understood that any trials to which lawyers worthy of their calling lend themselves will be trials in fact, not merely trials in name, to ratify a predetermined result." Our case, Your Honours, is about an outstanding military man, General Pavkovic, a career military man. In every evaluation he received in his career he got the highest possible marks. From 26 April 1998 to the start of the NATO campaign, there are 13 exhibits in this court case where General Pavkovic ordered adherence to international law or gave other clear indications of his determination that international law be honoured by those under his command. During the NATO campaign the record contains 25 similar exhibits, some very explicit in their wording. See, for instance, 4D411, 4D372, 4D189, and 4D158. He issued an average of one order or communication every three days during this campaign. It's difficult to argue that he did not take sufficient steps to prevent and punish crimes. I'd be surprised if any high-level commander in any recent world conflict has issued more such orders in an equivalent time than General Pavkovic did in this one. His arrest, his confinement, his conviction has been an enormous miscarriage of justice and I suggest politically motivated. This Chamber must correct this injustice. I think it may be helpful to begin with a comment about the Prosecution's theory of this case. Significant numbers of Kosovo residents left Kosovo during the NATO bombing. These included representatives of all ethnicities, including Serbs. This case really turned on the reason why Kosovo Albanians left Kosovo. Did they go out of fear of the fighting and the NATO bombing? Or were they forcefully expelled? The Prosecution theory is that they left because of the existence of a plan by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia leadership to forcibly expel a sufficient number of Kosovo Albanians to maintain Serbian control of the province. We said in our brief filed in September 2009 that 11 years had elapsed since those events in Kosovo and that during all those years not one document, not one witness has been found to provide any direct evidence of the existence of such a plan. It's now 14 and a half years with no such evidence surfacing. There simply could be no stronger evidence that the Prosecution theory is untrue and this failure after so much effort and so much time to find even one bit of direct evidence to support the theory. There's evidence that many left. There's evidence that some were forced to leave. But there's no evidence that these realities resulted from a still undiscovered plan to expel a sufficient number to maintain Serbian control of the province. On its face, the alleged plan defies logic. The world was watching. The UN Security Council had issued two Resolutions in 1998 regarding the events in Kosovo. International monitors were there after October 1998 when this plan was alleged to have been conceived. For this alleged plan to be real, one would need to suspend belief and conclude that a group of educated, intelligent persons, that being the FRY leadership, could have believed that they could have expelled thousands and thousands of Kosovo Albanians and then succeed on the international stage with an argument that these persons had never lived in Kosovo, that they were falsely claiming citizenship, that there had always been a Serbian majority living there. Not only was this theory not proved beyond a reasonable doubt; it was a theory that could not have been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. It was preposterous on its face, and yet it's the theory upon which this Trial Chamber based its conviction of General Pavkovic of joint criminal enterprise. Yesterday we heard the Prosecution say that the expulsions were done under the cover of NATO bombing. That sounds good, but then when you analyse it, what is "under the cover of NATO bombing"? That's probably the worst time possible because you've got NATO aircraft in the air overhead all the time, many of them surveillance aircraft, so they're seeing everything that's going on down there on the ground. They're bombing everything that's going on down there on the ground. We should have videos from NATO, from those aircraft, of people being expelled across the border, but there were none in this case. And "under the cover of NATO bombing" just doesn't make any sense either. I've suggested to you in my reference to the writings of Judge Jackson that this Trial Chamber approached the decision in this case with a result in mind but lacking evidence to support it. I don't make this charge lightly. I believe we can show you that it is, indeed, the case. We do not know how or why the failings that we're about to bring to your attention could have happened. It's not our place to try to make that determination. It's sufficient that we make you aware of them. I do know that the body of evidence in this case is enormous. We all worked under intense time pressures in this case, and since the trial we've actually discovered several exhibits we simply did not see before. The same time pressure could have caused the Trial Chamber to overlook some exhibits also. What I'm going to tell you about are numerous instances where the Trial Chamber in its judgement arrived at conclusions very damaging to General Pavkovic and essential to their conclusions which are not supported in the evidence cited in the footnotes attached to the conclusions. On their own without more, these make this judgement unsafe and not one that should be allowed to stand as a historical account of what happened in Kosovo and the role of General Pavkovic therein. It is not an honest judgement. It must be corrected, whether that is with a remand for a new trial or a reversal ordering acquittal of General Pavkovic of all charges. I want to refer very briefly to the Tribunal jurisprudence regarding what a reasoned judgement is. It was quoted in the recent Perisic decision at paragraph 92 from the Limaj Appeals Chamber and said: "The Appeals Chamber ... recalls that: "A Trial Chamber need not refer to the testimony of every witness or every piece of evidence on the trial record, 'as long as there is no indication that the Trial Chamber completely disregarded any particular piece of evidence.' Such disregard is shown 'when evidence which is clearly relevant to the findings is not addressed by the Trial Chamber's reasoning.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told that I have to speak slower, so I'll try to do that. The Prosecution's response brief to our main brief came as a surprise to me because in the 46 years that I've been working in criminal law, it was the first time that I'd seen a brief that had the footnotes refer to paragraphs of the judgement rather than the evidence in the case. I've always thought it was our obligation when communicating with a Court like this to refer to the evidence because the findings of the Trial Chamber are not evidence; they're simply findings that are supposed to be based on evidence. And then it happened again yesterday right here in court when the Prosecutor simply referred you to paragraphs of the judgement, not the underlying evidence that would support those paragraphs. And I can give you a couple of examples very quickly. In paragraph 91 of their response they talk about the Drewienkiewicz press release. We said it was based on information from the KLA. The OTP said in their brief that it was not, that it was based on what he saw, not what he heard. The press release which was not a press release was based on events in 1999, and the reference made by the OTP in their brief was to his statements about what he saw in 1998, not what he saw in 1999. I want to start with Volume I of the judgement, paragraph 1086. On 1 August of 1998, Pavkovic sent a request to the 3rd Army forward command post for authority to implement the third stage of the plan for combatting terrorism. That's P1419 of 1 August 1998. On the same day, Samardzic, his commander, ordered that the request be put on hold until his preliminary approval on 2 August and the president's approval on 3 August. The plan was not rejected; it was just delayed for about 48 hours. That's 4D125 of 1 August. On 2 August, Pavkovic directed Pristina Corps units toward the three main points involved, Drenica, Jablanica, and Smonica. And that's found at P1468, page 36, Joint Command notes. This is the activity, this -- mentioned by Pavkovic in the Joint Command, that the Trial Chamber concluded violated the Samardzic order. The Trial Chamber called it insubordination. Volume I, paragraph 1086. And then cited a document in support that was not even admitted into evidence, 4D458. However, two days earlier, on the 31st of July, Pavkovic was sent an order from the 3rd Army forward command post, General Simic, to use some of the Pristina Corps troops "to rout and destroy terrorist forces in the Smonica village sector, establishing full control of the sector, and ensuring safe use of the Djakovica-Batusa road." He was asked to brief Simic on specific plans to carry out this order at 1300 hours on 1 August at the forward command post. That is Exhibit 4D378, not cited by the Trial Chamber. The meeting apparently took place because General Simic in a 3rd Army combat report for 2 August 1998 reported that: "At 0500 hours on 2 August, the implementation started of our forces' planned activities in the Smonica and Jablanica villages sectors." This is from Exhibit 4DA3 of 2 August 1998 and is the very activity that Pavkovic reported in the Joint Command meeting on 2 August. The reference to Pavkovic's report to the Joint Command on 2 August is not a violation of a Samardzic order, but a report regarding the Simic order of 31 July. The Trial Chamber could not make this connection completely because Exhibit 4DA3 only became available after the judgement and was admitted by this Tribunal. This is a trial court error that is partly understandable. Another one is found Volume III, paragraph 779, footnote 1982. Our brief subground 1(C). The Prosecution's case against Pavkovic included a charge that he was involved in 1998 in the arming of the non-Albanian population and disarming the Kosovo Albanian population. We heard a lot about that yesterday. That finding was made by the Trial Chamber in agreement with the theory of the Prosecution. Clearly this finding was focused on arming of the civilian population since arming of military population is what military organisations do. The finding was based or the testimony was based on Exhibit P1415 of 26 June 1998. It's clear from the preamble that this was an order that came down from Samardzic to Pavkovic, ordering him to carry out its terms. And he was simply implementing this as ordered by his commander. It's also clear that those to be armed are "military conscripts," not non-Albanian civilians. The Trial Chamber's footnote cites Exhibit P1011 at page 58, which is a 23 July communication from Pavkovic to the collegium of 3rd Army commanders. He briefly mentions the arming of the population, but does not indicate any involvement himself or show any enthusiasm for it. He just says: "Despite the arming of the population, that factor in the system against terrorist struggle has not been fully included." The Trial Chamber then cites his statement to the Prosecution, P949. He was asked about the arming of the civilian population and he simply says that: "Albanians and Serbs were already armed 10 to 15 years ago ..." Nothing about his having anything to do with this arming situation. And that's all the evidence that's cited to support their conclusion, that Pavkovic was involved in the process of arming the non-Albanian population. Thus, in the evidence cited by the Chamber, there is no support for their conclusion and certainly no support for their conclusion in this paragraph that: "His enthusiasm for and involvement in these processes supports the Prosecution contention that Pavkovic acted in concert with members of the joint criminal enterprise to further the common purpose of maintaining control over Kosovo through various criminal means." Nothing in the evidence referred to by the Trial Chamber in footnote 1982 would suggest enthusiasm. They use that alleged enthusiasm from June and July of 1998 to conclude that it shows his acting in concert with members of the joint criminal enterprise, which was at least three months away from even being created according to the Prosecution's indictment. In Volume III, paragraph 667, footnote 1623, the Chamber concludes that: "Pavkovic's support and leadership of the process of arming the armed non-Albanian population is also demonstrated in discussions of the Joint Command on the issue throughout 1998." And that's just not so. You can go to every page of P1468, the Joint Command notes that are cited by the Trial Chamber, and you see no indication of Pavkovic's support and leadership for the process of arming. It's mentioned on occasion by other persons, he's present there, but he says not a word. The clear purpose to the Trial Chamber conclusions regarding the arming process was to provide support for the proposition that it was this arming and Pavkovic's part in it and enthusiastic support for it that contributed to the goals of the joint criminal enterprise once the war started on 24 March 1999. In other words, the armed non-Albanian civilians supported the plan and played an important role in assisting the VJ and Pavkovic in its implementation. And we'll see that the TC attempts to support this claim but fails to do so. And I think in that view it's interesting to point out some testimony by Dimitrijevic who the Trial Chamber thought was a good witness. He said: "We didn't have any cases where civilians misused the weapons they'd been issued with. In other words, I'm talking about them using weapons for any other purpose. It simply served to protect those people against any terrorist acts. That was the purpose of these weapons." That's transcript 26635. I go now to Volume III, paragraph 490, footnote 1064 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask counsel to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In this paragraph the Trial Chamber concludes: "Although the armed non-Albanian population did not form part of the VJ, the VJ nonetheless was involved in arming and organising this entity and ordered its engagement during joint operations with the MUP in 1999." In footnote 1064, the Chamber first cites P2086 of 1 July 1998. There's nothing in this document that supports VJ involvement in arming, organising, or ordering engagement. TC cites P1114, again nothing in this document supports their conclusion of arming and assisting. They cite the testimony of Pesic at page T 7316. It has nothing to do with the Trial Chamber conclusion. They cite the statement of Nike Peraj, P2253 at paragraph 15. It does not support the conclusion in any way. Finally the Trial Chamber cites 3D1087, a document issued on 8 April 1999, and again there's absolutely no support. If the Trial Chamber concern about this subject was merited, then one would have expected to see reports of armed non-Albanians expelling, slaughtering, committing crimes against Kosovo Albanians in large numbers. Such reports simply do not exist. Volume III, paragraph 775, footnote 1971, deals with the issue of intent. In paragraph 775, the Trial Chamber talked about how the information in Pavkovic's possession regarding the commission of crimes by VJ subordinates and MUP members and his continuing ordering of joint operations was evidence of his intent that such crimes occur and, by extension, his attempt to participate in the alleged joint criminal enterprise. Part of the Trial Chamber effort to establish Pavkovic's knowledge of crimes being committed by the VJ in 1999 was the finding in this paragraph that he attended a meeting in Pristina with Stevanovic and Djordjevic from the MUP: "While Kosovo Albanians were being forcibly displaced from the town by VJ and MUP forces acting together." The only cite is to one page of the testimony of Lazarevic, where he says that this meeting occurred on 19 April 1999. The Trial Chamber provides no support for the proposition that VJ and MUP forces were expelling Kosovo Albanians at the time and that Pavkovic was aware of it. So the question is: Is there any credible evidence in the record, even though uncited by the Trial Chamber, that would support such conclusion? And I suggest to you there is not. A review of Volume I, paragraphs 838 through 873, where the Chamber describes the evidence of persons leaving Pristina, there's not one bit of evidence that VJ and MUP were engaged in forcible displacements there on 19 April, when Pavkovic was there and was alleged to have seen this happen. So the Trial Chamber must have known from their conclusions in Volume I that there was no support for their conclusion in Volume III. The only reference in April in these paragraphs in Volume I is in paragraph 867 where it is reported that a witness, SD3, testified that he saw the greatest number of people leaving Pristina in the second half of April after the post office was bombed. He said MUP and VJ were not forcing persons to leave; they were leaving on their own. The testimony of Witness Filipovic also sheds light on this issue. Filipovic basically said that he was in the Pristina Corps command post there from 29 March on, that there were no Pristina Corps combat units in the Pristina area after the NATO bombing started because they were heavy targets in the Pristina area and they, according to plan, left Pristina and went to safer places. From 30 March 1999 to 10 June, Kumanovo Agreement, not a single member of the Pristina garrison fired a single bullet despite daily attacks on Pristina by terrorists. So the Trial Chamber's proposition that Pavkovic knew of crimes in 1999 because he was present in Pristina on 19 April when VJ and MUP forces were expelling people is totally without evidentiary foundation. In Volume III, paragraph 775, again deals with awareness of crimes in 1998. In this paragraph the Chamber concluded that: "Reports from international sources made him," Pavkovic, "aware of MUP and VJ involvement in the forcible displacement and commission of crimes against Kosovo Albanians, including in Pristina where he was regularly located." The cited source for this conclusion was a press statement and testimony by Drewienkiewicz. The so-called press statement is P2542. It's clearly not a press statement. It doesn't say "press release" on it or anything like that. In his testimony at T 7815, he did not say it was a press statement; he agreed with the Prosecution's suggestion that "it's a press statement that you gave or your note for a statement you gave." There's no indication it ever was released to the media, no indication that it was published in any media. There's no exhibit of any media publication of this alleged press release. However, the Chamber's conclusion necessarily implies that it was a press release, that it was actually released to the press, that it was published in some publication, that General Pavkovic read that publication and thus knew of its contents. There's simply no evidence of that at all beyond the mere existence of this document, which I submit to you was not even a press release. Volume III, paragraph 572, footnote 1336, deals with the underreporting of crime, which he was accused of by the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. In this paragraph the Trial Chamber says: "Farkas, chief of the security administration of VJ in 1999 testified that also as a consequence of the revelation of the underreporting of crimes, Ojdanic sent him on a mission as head of the security administration to inspect the security organs in the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps on 5 and 6 May 1999." This is footnote 1336, citing the testimony of Farkas at 16292. And here's what the testimony really was: "Q. Thank you, General. Why did you in early May go to Kosovo? Could you please tell us? "A. Well, the first reason was that we had a situation there. Some information was not specific enough, especially as regards security affairs. And then the Chief of the General Staff, or rather, of the Supreme Command Staff ordered me to go down to Kosovo and see where the problem lay because he suspected that those reports were not reaching him regularly and he thought that what he was getting was not sufficient for his decision-making." Nothing in this testimony says that he was sent there "as a consequence of the revelation of the underreporting of crimes." He only said that there was a situation regarding security affairs. Again with regard to underreporting, Volume III, paragraph 572, footnote 1340. This deals with two witnesses, Aleksandar Vasiljevic and Branko Gajic, they were both assigned to the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff and were deputy chief and assistant chief respectively. In this paragraph the Chamber said this: "Vasiljevic gave evidence that he later discovered that a decision had been taken by the 3rd Army command not to report the occurrence of certain crimes in regular combat reports, as they were being dealt with by military judicial organs." So they're saying basically that Pavkovic issued an order not to report crimes based on this testimony of Vasiljevic. They repeated the same thing in paragraph 737, indicating the importance they attach to it. Now, this is a serious finding by the Trial Chamber, a finding that Pavkovic made a decision not to report crimes, to hide them from his superiors. If it's true, it would support a finding that not only did Pavkovic know of crimes being committed in 1999, he was deliberately not reporting them up the chain of command. So it becomes important to see exactly what Vasiljevic says he discovered on his mission to Kosovo. He and Gajic were sent there in the first week of June, transcript 8751. The testimony cited in footnote 1340 of the Chamber is in part this from TC 8750. This is Vasiljevic answering questions: "Then I asked the chief of security in the Pristina Corps whether he had sent that information to the security section of the 3rd Army ... and the chief of security of the Pristina Corps said that he had not reported because all those cases had been processed already. "And that's what I told him, that it was just a pretext, an attempt at self-justification, that he should have made the report along the line of the security organs, if not otherwise, and he should have also reported to the security section of the 3rd Army in Nis." And then he went on to say: "But I must say that those cases were not covered up or concealed; that was my impression. They didn't report it the way I suggested because the cases had already been prosecuted and processed. They simply thought the problem had been resolved, the perpetrators had been arrested and that's why they committed this omission in reporting." So what he actually reported was that the chief of security of the Pristina Corps, one level below General Pavkovic, had not reported this information up to the 3rd Army, had simply not reported it at all. And the Trial Chamber concludes from that that General Pavkovic ordered that crimes not be reported. And there's simply zero evidence to support that conclusion, none. Volume III, paragraph 651, footnote 1567. The Prosecution contended that -- and the Trial Chamber agreed that Pavkovic had a special relationship with Milosevic that enabled him to go around the chain of command and, in effect, be the man in charge in Kosovo even as Samardzic was his superior in the 3rd Army command. The Trial Chamber's acceptance of this proposition can be seen in the language used in this paragraph. Volume III, paragraph 651, the Trial Chamber finds in a letter of 22 July 1998: "Pavkovic reminded Samardzic that the plan for combatting terrorism had been agreed in a meeting with the FRY president and then," and this is an important word, "then directed Samardzic to draw up details of the Pristina Corps operations." This meeting was attended not just by Pavkovic, but by Samardzic and several other individuals, but the important language here, the Trial Chamber uses the word "directed," indicating that Pavkovic was ordering Samardzic to do something. Actually, the word used by Pavkovic was "please," not "directed." The document begins with the heading: "Clarification required ..." and ends with: "Please work out in more detail the engagement of the Pristina Corps units in the implementation of the plan." That's 4D100 of 22 July 1998. What the document does is reminds Samardzic of a meeting in Belgrade, express a need for instructions as to what to do with the Pristina Corps as a result of that meeting, and asks very politely for those instructions. Pavkovic was not entitled to engage the VJ based on the meeting in Belgrade with Milosevic; he needed specific orders from his commander, Samardzic. It is clearly a document showing that Samardzic was in command and Pavkovic was asking for his next instructions. The testimony of Vasiljevic in this regard at T 9092 is illustrative. On the same day Samardzic responded and suggested that since the plan adopted by Milosevic had been initially proposed by Pavkovic, he would like him to draft very specifically a proposal for indirect and direct engagement of Pristina Corps units in blocking the villages of Junik and Jasic and unblocking the said roads. That's 4D119, 22 July 1998. There has been some concern expressed about this plan having been drafted by Pavkovic and that would show some kind of a close relationship between he and Milosevic, but just being realistic about this from a military point of view, if someone is going to be asked to draft a plan regarding actions that need to be taken in a combat area, like was going on in Kosovo, wouldn't you want the person that is there, that's familiar with the territory, that's familiar with the villages, that's familiar with everything that's going on, to make a suggestion as to a plan to deal with those issues and that's exactly what happened here. They picked the right person to make the proposal because he was the one that knew everything. Anyhow, the next day Pavkovic submitted his proposal, again using the word "please," in asking Samardzic for approval. That's 4D101 of 23 July. And on the same day Samardzic then approved but did not allow the use of Pristina Corps units in unblocking the Pristina-Kijevo-Pec and Stimlje-Dulje-Suva Reka roads. That's 4D102 of 23 July. The Trial Chamber then found that this order "asserted the obligation to adhere to the VJ chain of command," leaving one with the belief that somewhere Samardzic told Pavkovic that he had to adhere to the VJ chain of command, as if he was not adhering to the VJ chain of command, which he was, by the way. And this conclusion is not supported by anything. That's in paragraph 651. Nothing supports it at all. Next is Volume III, paragraph 514, the footnote is 1133. It has to do with the violation of the October Agreements that Pavkovic was charged with by the Prosecution and found to have been guilty of by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber says in Volume III, paragraph 514, that Dimitrijevic, who they found to be a truthful witness in spite of significant evidence to the contrary, reported to the General Staff in late 1998 and early 1999 that reports from the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps that all actions occurring in Kosovo were defensive were both incorrect and misleading. The Chamber cites P928 of 30 December 1998 at page 14, where Dimitrijevic is complaining of a situation near Podujevo, where it is reported that the VJ was attacked while engaging in a planned exercise. He says it was not a planned exercise but an effort to provoke the KLA so that the MUP could respond. The Trial Chamber under the heading "Conduct with respect to the October Agreements" quoted the Dimitrijevic charges as evidence of violation of the October Agreements by Pavkovic. They printed this quote from Dimitrijevic: "After the so-called pretend or real planned exercises in which this company took part in the field, General," this is a collegium meeting, by the way, and he's talking to General Perisic, I think, "General, these sorts of moves will lead us to disaster. The explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do." That's paragraph 514. Without more, this tends to make the case that reports from the Pristina Corps or 3rd Army regarding this incident contained lies and misinformation, claiming this was a planned exercise when it was not, instead a provocation. But there's more that the Chamber apparently chose not to mention because it would destroy the point they were trying to make. The footnote 1133 directs the reader to the testimony of Dimitrijevic at pages 26627, and 26653 to 26654, but fails to point out his testimony at T 26631. And this is really important. On this page Judge Bonomy asks Dimitrijevic about Exhibit P928 and reads to him that quote about this not being a planned exercise and that the reports were not true. This appears in paragraph 514 of the judgement, and it is in response to Judge Bonomy's question that Dimitrijevic then says: "... I know that soon after this things were checked, and General Obradovic explained that after an additional report was requested they established that, after all, this was not a provocation; rather, it was a planned exercise ..." So on the same page of the transcript where Judge Bonomy reads this quote from Dimitrijevic that the Trial Chamber relied on, that this was not a planned exercise, on the same page of the transcript Dimitrijevic says: We learned later that it was a planned exercise. That didn't make it into the Trial Chamber's account of this matter. So with the clear testimony that Dimitrijevic's allegations at this collegium meeting were wrong, the Chamber chose to use the allegations as if they were true, leaving out the testimony that it was, in fact, a planned exercise. Volume III, paragraph 1161, again dealing with violation of the October Agreements. This regards the issue of the MP battalion of the 72nd Special Brigade being moved into Kosovo without Ojdanic's approval. The Trial Chamber said that at a collegium meeting - and we talk about that much later - but the Trial Chamber said at a meeting of the collegium: "Ojdanic told those present that he would have a talk with Pavkovic about the matter." The citation is in footnote 1161 to pages 16 and 24 of P941. This language or anything like it is simply not there. From the judgement it appears that Ojdanic was concerned and was going to talk to Pavkovic about this. There's simply no evidence that we could find to support that conclusion, certainly not where the Chamber said it was found in their footnote. Volume III, paragraph 659, at footnote 1595, deals with the issue of clashes with superiors that the Trial Chamber found Pavkovic was involved in. Paragraph 659 they've said this: "On 6 September 1998, Samardzic and Pavkovic also clashed over a request made by Pavkovic to make a helicopter available to the Pristina Corps." There simply was no clash. It's clear from a reading of the relevant documents that's covered in detail at paragraph 116 of our brief, the Trial Chamber was simply wrong. The Exhibit is 4D230. You can look at it. What it is is an exhibit where Pavkovic asks for a helicopter. The request has to be sent to the General Staff by Samardzic. He sends it to the General Staff. He gets a response back from the General Staff denying it, and then informs Pavkovic of the process that has to be undertaken to get approval, has to go through the air force, and that sort of thing. So that's all there was to that; there was no clash at all. And the contention that there was such close relationship between Pavkovic and Milosevic, if that was true, he wouldn't have had to go through this anyhow. He could have just called Milosevic and said: Send me a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You talk about arming or disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The breaching of the October Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As well as introducing troops to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: All this happened in 1998 and early 1999. My question is: What is your position on the issue whether in the circumstances of the present case a joint criminal enterprise member can be found to have acted in furtherance of the common purpose prior to the time when it was found to have existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position is that he can't. The simple answer is: That can't be. And I do intend to go into that in a little bit of detail in a few minutes, but to answer your question: No, I don't think that can happen. But the Trial Chamber made all of these findings and the Trial Chamber concluded that these findings were very important to their determination of the existence of the joint criminal enterprise and General Pavkovic's intent to operate within it. So I think it's important for me to bring the 1998 matters to your attention. We concluded from the very beginning of this case that the 1998 matters were irrelevant, should not be allowed into evidence, that they were not in the indictment, and the Trial Chamber basically agreed with us but then said that the Prosecution could use it in very limited ways with very exact proof. So that's what happened. And I've always been frustrated by the fact that we spent so much time on 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm looking forward to your further elaborations of this issue at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Volume III, paragraph 694, 704, 774, were all based on an exhibit, a document, 4D103. And the Trial Chamber's findings were based on the proposition that this was an active order, issued by Pavkovic, ordering the engagement in 1999, Your Honour, of VJ troops. In Volume III, paragraph 694, the Trial Chamber says this: "An order issued by Pavkovic on 23 March 1999 directed that the VJ was to be immediately engaged against all enemy forces," immediately engaged against all enemy forces. It further stated that: "In places or sectors where the presence of the KLA has been established, units were to establish protective shell in order to prevent attacks on the 3rd Army commands and units, to focus on populated places with a loyal population, and to prevent a link-up between KLA and NATO air-borne assaults." We talk about this in our brief at paragraph 214, but there's some additional clarification I wanted to give you. The cite, as I said was to 4D103, it's paragraph 1.6 of 23 March 1999. This is reported under the heading "Military Orders" -- the Trial Chamber's heading, "Military Orders," seeking to set out the orders issued by Pavkovic during the NATO invasion. It was part of the fabric on which the Trial Chamber stitched the guilt of Pavkovic. However, as is much too common in this judgement, the Trial Chamber was simply wrong. The order was not what the Trial Chamber says it was. The Trial Chamber left out the main operative language of the order that was its very first phrase, which is this: "At the beginning of NATO strikes and in case of communications break with superior commands and officers," do this. So the order was only to be implemented in case of communications break with superior commands. It wasn't an order for an immediate engagement at all. It was only to be operative in the event of this break and only during the duration of this break, and it never took effect because the communication break never happened. The Trial Chamber repeated this error in paragraph 704, again citing this document as if it were an operative order. Here the Trial Chamber said: "It was a basis for the Joint Command orders for the VJ and MUP to engage in widespread joint operations in late March of 1999." And finally in paragraph 774, using the same document as a basis to conclude that in spite of his awareness of allegations of widespread criminal activity, he ordered VJ operations in conjunction with MUP. Of course, the order was not activated and, further, it does not call for joint activities with MUP. The Trial Chamber must have been aware of the Lazarevic Pristina Corps order in response to this, 5D1793 of 23 March, where Pavkovic's paragraph 1.6 becomes Lazarevic's paragraph 1.6 with only minor changes. The Lazarevic version orders that it goes into effect only if there is a severance of communications with the Pristina Corps command. Again, never happened. The Trial Chamber must also have been aware of an order issued by the command of the 125th Motorised Brigade on 24 March 1999, 5D708, limiting the order to the event that there's a communication breakdown with the brigade command. The contingency of the order goes all the way down to the brigades and never took effect. Volume III, paragraph 705, footnote 1736, this deals with the close relationship with Milosevic. The Trial Chamber spoke of testimony by General Curcin regarding the drafting of document P1487, a group of suggestions from Ojdanic to Pavkovic regarding a Pristina Corps Joint Command order for an action near Rugova gorge. The Joint Command/Pristina Command order was issued on 15 April 1999 at P1878. Note that at the very beginning this document refers to a map, and it's also important to note that this is not a 3rd Army command order; it's a command not issued by Pavkovic but a command of General Lazarevic at the Pristina Corps command. Basically Curcin testified that he was contacted by Ojdanic who said he had seen Pavkovic and was given the map for the ordered operations. Ojdanic said that he saw Pavkovic after Pavkovic had been to a meeting with Milosevic. The Trial Chamber says: "Curcin further testified that Pavkovic came to see Ojdanic after meeting with Milosevic: "Having bypassed his immediate superior ..." They say this is testimony of Curcin, paragraph 705. Curcin doesn't say this, he doesn't say that it was a bypass of his immediate superior. The Trial Chamber again is wrong. Footnote 1736, the reference to the testimony of Curcin 17025, 17027 of the transcript. There's no evidence of what Pavkovic and Milosevic talked about, if they actually met on that day, none whatsoever. The Trial Chamber suggests that Ojdanic's sending suggestions to Pavkovic is quite irregular since he was his superior and could simply have ordered him to proceed in a certain way, and that is certainly true, he could have. However, these suggestions went to Pavkovic who did not issue the original orders. They were issued at the corps level by the Pristina Corps. We believe this is simply a consultation between two military leaders regarding activities to be carried out by the Pristina Corps in Kosovo and the best way for them to be carried out. Two superior minds meeting about a matter of major concern, and suggestions from Ojdanic in that situation are not irregular at all. Volume III, paragraph 729, deals with the failure to prevent or punish. The Trial Chamber complains in this paragraph that: "Reports from the 3rd Army command to the Supreme Command Staff at the start of April 1999 indicate that many criminal and disciplinary proceedings had been initiated for crimes against the VJ but did not mention any specific investigations of war crimes or serious violent crimes." I suggest this would only be of evidentiary significance if the Trial Chamber had been also referred to evidence that the 3rd Army was in possession of specific information regarding "investigations of war crimes or serious violent crimes" and failed to report this information. This they do not do. They don't cite any evidence of that regard that was not reported. They do say this, that two 3rd Army combat reports "state that crimes of looting from abandoned houses of Kosovo Albanians had occurred." That's in footnote 1826. And they cite two exhibits, 4D274 and 4D275. And you can look at those and you won't see any evidence of looting from abandoned houses of Kosovo Albanians. It's not mentioned in these documents at all. The only information about houses in one of those documents is in 4D275, where it's reported that NATO aircraft attacked two villages, damaging houses and causing casualties among the civilian population. That's on page 2. Whether the casualties and houses were Serb or Albanian is not mentioned. Volume III, paragraph 179 at footnote 1785, this has to do with Pavkovic's awareness of 1999 crimes. In an effort to show this awareness by units under his command in 1999, the Trial Chamber said: "By 31 March, Pavkovic had information indicating that VJ military territorial units and MUP forces were channelling displaced Kosovo Albanians to Albania." The Trial Chamber cites as their source for that P2930, a 31 March report, from a Pristina Corps command group at Mazrek village to the Pristina Corps operations centre. The Trial Chamber cited no evidence that this report went beyond the command operations centre of the Pristina Corps. The document doesn't show that it went anywhere but to the Pristina Corps command. It did not go to the Pristina Corps operations centre. Looking at the Pristina Corps combat reports that did go to the 3rd Army operations centre for that day and the next day, there's no indication that this information was forwarded to the 3rd Army. 6D1135 for 31 March, 4D371 for 1 April. Thus, there's simply no evidence that Pavkovic was ever made aware of this information in that report from Mazrek village. No proof that he had this by March 31, as the Trial Chamber declares. What he did know by the 31st of March is information contained in a 3rd Army combat report, 4D510 of 24 March, regarding a column of refugees seeking to cross the border. VJ border security closed the border, did not permit them to leave the country. Now, the Trial Chamber was aware of this report, they cited it. After mentioning at paragraph 556 [sic] in Volume III, their conclusion was that VJ was "involved with the movement of the civilian population." They didn't say that that movement was to keep them from going across the border; they just said "involved with the movement," leaving the impression that they must have been involved with expelling Kosovo Albanians. That is not what happened. We think this casts a serious doubt on a plan that had supposedly existed since at least October to expel Kosovo Albanians. It makes such a conclusion beyond a reasonable doubt, I think, an impossible conclusion to reach. I want to go now to the questions that the Chamber asked us to address, and I'm going to start with this. We were asked to address this: "Discuss, with reference to the record, whether there would be any effect on Pavkovic's appeal regarding his convictions pursuant to JCE III, if the Appeals Chamber were to accept the Prosecution's argument that the Trial Chamber applied an incorrect mens rea standard for JCE III liability." The simple answer, Your Honours, is no. Consider the following example: General A, as a member of a joint criminal enterprise, orders a unit under his command to expel the inhabitants of a village from the country to force them to flee to a neighbouring country. He recognises that since the soldiers under his command are typical of young soldiers everywhere, there is a possibility that they will commit other criminal acts in the process of carrying out this order. He does not intend for that to happen. He does not wish for that to happen. He wants to prevent that from happening. So he issues orders to be brought to the attention of all the soldiers that contain an assurance that they would be arrested and imprisoned for the commission of any crimes during the ordered exercise. He orders their immediate superiors to monitor the activities to prevent any such crimes and immediately take action to punish any violator. This is the commander's responsibility under international law and as set out in Article 7 of the Statute of this Tribunal. Article 7 refers to the crimes defined in Articles 2 through 5 of the Statute. Joint criminal enterprise under current Tribunal jurisprudence is simply a form of commission of those stated crimes and thus Article 7 is applicable. Joint criminal enterprise is not, as we all know, set out as some separate offence. Article 7 makes a superior responsible for the acts of a subordinate if it is shown that the superior has failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. It thus makes no difference to our position in our brief regarding the convictions of Pavkovic under the third category of joint criminal enterprise which mens rea standard is applied. The difference between the Pavkovic facts and the examples set out above is that the example presumes a commander who as part of a joint criminal enterprise ordered the commission of the offence that was its purpose. No joint criminal enterprise was proved in this case, Pavkovic was not a member of any joint criminal enterprise, Pavkovic never issued an order to soldiers under his command to commit any offence punishable by this Tribunal. He made extraordinary efforts to prevent the commission of any crimes, both as commander of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army. The second question we were asked to: "Discuss, with reference to the record, whether, in the event the Appeals Chamber were to grant the Prosecution's argument that the sexual assaults of K62, K14, and K31 constituted persecutions, Pavkovic should be held responsible for these persecutions pursuant to JCE III." Again, my answer is no. Even if the correct interpretation of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal with regard to JCE III is that argued by the Prosecution, General Pavkovic could not be held responsible for the sexual assaults that are the subject of this question. Assuming the finding that there was a joint criminal enterprise and that Pavkovic was a member of it, there would need to be proof that he could have foreseen the possibility that these offences would be committed by those carrying out his orders. That requires a connection to be shown between Pavkovic and the principals in these offences. If they were not individuals who were members of units under his command, then he could not possibly foresee that they would commit these crimes. With regard to persecution, there is simply no evidence that could be called "proof beyond a reasonable doubt" that these incidents were persecutory in nature other than simple non-war crime sexual assaults. With regard to K31 there is no evidence regarding the identity of the three soldiers who committed the assault. She describes their uniforms as green camouflage, some had their faces painted black and wore bandannas bearing the word "massacre" written on them. That's P2596, page 1. One had a beard clear down to his chest, T 9250. Their descriptions are consistent with paramilitaries, not VJ soldiers. As Witness K73 pointed out in his testimony, regular VJ soldiers were not allowed to wear beards. That's transcript 3310. It is certainly not shown that these were VJ soldiers in the chain of command flowing down from General Pavkovic and among those who would have received Pavkovic's orders regarding adherence to international humanitarian law. The events that are described are strongly consistent with the non-persecutory attack just as they could be consistent with a persecutory one. But when there are two reasonable conclusions, the one that's consistent with innocence must be the one that's chosen. Witness K62's testimony does not identify the three men who sexually assaulted her beyond brown and green camouflage uniforms, wearing hats with masks on their faces. That's transcript 2274, 75. She said she was staying home that day because she was afraid of paramilitaries, 2269. This confirms that paramilitaries were present in Pristina at that time. There's actually no evidence that the attack on this witness was persecutory in nature. There's no evidence as to who the men were who attacked her. The fact that persons who committed these offences were wearing uniforms is not at all conclusive as to the military organisations, if any, that they may have belonged to. As Zlatomir Pesic testified: "There were army surplus sale points where uniforms and parts of uniforms were available to be bought and that's how people could get hold of a uniform, not only by having a prior war-time assignment." Transcript 7316.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is kindly asked to slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: K14 gives a clear description of being sexually assaulted by a policeman. She even gives his name. There may be no contest over whether this person was actually a policeman. Clearly he was not a VJ soldier in the Pavkovic chain of command. There's nothing that would make this attack a persecution beyond a reasonable doubt. Finally, in paragraph 11, Volume III of the judgement, the Trial Chamber points out that the Prosecution was only proceeding on the basis that the members of the joint criminal enterprise used members of the forces of FRY and Serbia that they had control over to carry out the deportations, forced transfers, murders, and persecutions. With regard to these three events, the Prosecution failed to prove which member or members of the JCE had control over these perpetrators or whether any did or that they were even members of the forces of FRY and Serbia. We were asked to: "Discuss the relevance of the indictment made public on 27 May 1999 on the mens rea of Sainovic and Pavkovic, given that the indictment was made public after the last crime for which Sainovic and Pavkovic were convicted was committed on 25 May 1999." We believe the answer is that it had absolutely no relevance. There's absolutely no evidence as to when or even whether Pavkovic became aware of this indictment. The Trial Chamber's finding in Volume III, paragraph 755 that Pavkovic "must have been informed of the existence of the indictment on or around 27 May" has absolutely no evidentiary basis, none. It's pure speculation and not a speculation upon which the TC could base knowledge of allegations that crimes had been committed by VJ personnel. In paragraph 755 the Chamber says: "The indictment was discussed at the Supreme Command Staff briefing of 28 May where Branko Krga stated that one of the purposes of bringing the indictment against the high FRY Serbian officials was to stall peace initiatives." Now, if you just read that, the conclusion that you draw is that there was a discussion, a discussion means more than one person talking. And that Krga said it had something to do with high FRY Serbian officials. Now, this is a stretch without evidentiary support, another one. If you actually look at 3D628 and read about this "discussion" that was had at that meeting between the attendees, you'd very disappointed. It does show that taking anything that the Trial Chamber says for granted can be a big mistake. There is no indication that there was any discussion of the Milosevic indictment made public the day before. It was not mentioned by name. No one says anything about an indictment against high FRY Serbian officials. The only thing is this. Branko Krga says: "Bringing an indictment has several purposes. One of them is, of course, stalling peace initiatives." That's it. That's all that was said at that meeting by Branko Krga. While it's highly likely that this is the ICTY indictment that Krga mentions, it's no evidence whatsoever that it had been seen by any of the members of the Supreme Command Staff, studied by them, discussed by them. To conclude that this small phrase represented awareness within the VJ and that "Pavkovic must have been informed of the existence of the indictment on or around 27 May" is nothing more than pure speculation. And yet, it's used along with other evidence to prove that Pavkovic was aware of allegations of crimes committed by VJ personnel. We were asked to: "Discuss, as a legal matter as well as with respect to the particular Trial Chamber's findings for each appellant convicted of JCE I, whether the actus reus and mens rea of a JCE member may be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose of the JCE." And I agree with the Prosecution when they said yesterday that it does not. One of the problems with regard to analysis of this issue is the language of the indictment. In paragraph 20 it charges: "This joint criminal enterprise came into existence no later than October 1998 and continued throughout the time-period when the crimes alleged in Counts 1 to 5 of this indictment occurred, beginning on or about January 1999 and continuing until 20 June 1999." It's difficult to figure out - if there was a joint criminal enterprise - when it might have come into existence. There's certainly no evidence that one existed at any time and certainly no evidence that there was anything going on in October of 1998 that would have caused the creation of a joint criminal enterprise. What was going on from October right up to almost the day that NATO attacked was efforts to solve the problem in many different forms. And I suggest that the government of FRY was making serious efforts to solve that problem. And it was almost done at Rambouillet, they had an agreement, and then at the last minute, as you'll see, they brought in this Military Agreement that the Serbs simply couldn't accept. Had the Prosecution been able to prove and had the Trial Chamber concluded that the JCE alleged in the indictment was in existence in October 1998, that would compel one answer. However, it's impossible to tell. Well, it is possible to tell. I take that back. The plan as alleged was an expulsion plan. It seems to me that it would be virtually impossible to form an intent to participate in such a plan before it actually came into existence. We strongly contend that there was no plan, no JCE, theoretically, if such a plan came into existence with a pattern of crimes in 1999. Nothing Pavkovic was doing before that date could have been found to be the mens rea for the carrying out of the plan. Up until 13 January 1999, Pavkovic was the commander of the Pristina Corps. What the Prosecution alleged and what the Chamber found and what the evidence actually showed about his tenure there will be discussed as we proceed. So the shorter answer is that one cannot intend to carry out the goals of a plan when there is no plan. It must exist before intent to carry it out can be formed. We were asked to: "Discuss whether and under what circumstances the mens rea under JCE I for deportation and other inhumane acts ... may be inferred from the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including crimes other than deportation and other inhumane acts (forcible transfer)." The allegations and findings regarding deportations in this case all deal with events following the beginning of the NATO bombing on 24 March 1999. The Court's question is: Could Pavkovic's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998 be used to infer a mens rea for the deportations that were the goal of the alleged JCE? There are circumstances where I suppose that could be the case. If the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt were to show the existence of an expulsion plan satisfying the actus reus of JCE I during the 1998 criminal events in which Pavkovic was aware and if during that time these criminal events were seen as preparatory to carrying out the joint plan, then the inference could be made. The evidence in this case, however, does not come close to supporting such a finding. The OTP effectively admits as much by their indictment, that alleges expulsions in accordance with the alleged plan, beginning with the NATO bombing. We were asked to: "Discuss whether the incident in Tusilje ... on 29 March 1999 should have been pleaded in the indictment, whether a defect in this respect, if any, was cured, and whether Sainovic, Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic suffered a prejudice as a result of any such defect." We believe that clearly the Trial Chamber should not have convicted Pavkovic based upon a finding of deportation or forcible transfer from the village of Tusilje. We have no reason, however, to believe that this defect was cured in any way. It's impossible to determine if General Pavkovic suffered any prejudice as a result. I want to talk now for just a few moments about the common plan, the existence of the common plan. This is subground (B), 1(B) of our brief. It has to do with expulsion of Kosovo Albanians. Exhibit 2D301, which was not cited by the Trial Chamber, of 7 April 1999 is an announcement from the FRY government urging Kosovo Albanians not to leave the country. This militates against the existence of an expulsion plan. Voluntary departure would be much more effective in realising such an alleged plan if it existed. So would the leaders plead against voluntary departure just so they could forcibly expel? It makes no sense. The Trial Chamber didn't cite this document. On the same day, 7 April, 3D753, the office of the General Staff issued a plea to the Albanian population to return to their homes. The Trial Chamber didn't cite this document. Just eight days after these pleas from the government and military for the Kosovo Albanians to remain in the country, General William Walker went to the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing and secured an agreement with the border organs in Macedonia that they would let all Albanian refugees into the country without any hold-up. In other words, kind of assisting that process of refugees leaving the country. That's 4D511, again not mentioned by the Trial Chamber. It's a 15 April 1999 document. On 21 April 1999, in 3D431, again not mentioned by the Trial Chamber, a Pristina Military District combat report to the Pristina Corps reports NATO projectiles hitting a refugee camp, completely demolishing it, and killing and wounding the refugees. News of such an attack, it seems to me, would certainly heighten fears of NATO bombing and cause people to want to flee. This report just a couple of weeks after the government pleas for Kosovo Albanians to remain additionally says that many Albanian families were returning to the Podujevo area, some with the assistance of MUP. Again the TC didn't mention this. So why did they leave? That's a major question. Why did they leave? We're all citizens of this world. We see what's going on around this world every day. We see what goes on in places like Iraq and Afghanistan and now in Syria, all the refugees that leave those places in a state of war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speaker to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm having trouble speaking slowly enough. I'm sorry. We see what happens in this world, and we see no allegations of expulsion in any of these other situations where refugees are leaving in large numbers. Serb refugees left in large numbers during the NATO bombing. Helpful can be the testimony of Zyrapi, the KLA officer and Chief of Staff of the KLA. At transcript 5992, he talks about the KLA wanting the population to move for security reasons on 25 March, the day after the NATO bombing started. 5D980 is a Pristina Military District combat report to the 3rd Army. In the first paragraph they report NATO bombing in the area and the results, and then in the same paragraph they report that both Albanians and Serbs are leaving. Albanians going to Macedonia, Serbs going to Nis. Serbs would not have been leaving because of an expulsion plan; they would have been leaving because of the NATO bombing. It makes it hard to argue that Albanians were leaving due to expulsion. The Trial Chamber ignored this aspect of this document. On 3 April 1999 Bozidar Delic, commander of the 549th VJ Motorised Brigade, sent a report to the Pristina Corps command, which is 5D885. This report was stamped "Military Secret: Strictly confidential." Most of these reports were stamped with that. Most of these reports were confidential. No one expected them to see the light of day. They weren't done for PR purposes; they're real. Commander Delic had no reason to suspect that his report would be made public. It gives it a certain aura of credibility, significantly more so than after-the-fact testimony or public statements by persons from either side of this conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you have trouble to speak slow enough, you may make a longer pause after each sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The report was sent just a few days after the beginning of the NATO bombing. Delic pointed out his surprise at the huge numbers of refugees, 290.000 since the bombing started. He pointed out that he had learned that it was the position of authorities to keep them from leaving, to have them return to their homes. He said the refugees were coming from the remotest parts of Kosovo. He said persons in his brigade had talked with the refugees and they gave their reasons for wanting to leave and leaving, and he listed those reasons. A, fear of major fighting; B, some to avoid forced mobilisation into the KLA; C, fear of the army and the police, especially Arkan's troops. However, on further questioning they said they did not fear the army. They would stay if army troops were near where they lived. And finally, D, the NATO bombing was emphasised by all groups as the primary reason because NATO does not distinguish between troops and civilians. They do not look where they are striking. There is no indication that anyone was being forcibly deported. Although cited several times, the Trial Chamber gave the conclusions of this document no credit. On the other hand, Kosovo Albanian witnesses in the refugees camps and in court had a motive for being untruthful about their reasons for departure. Everyone knew that Kosovo was seeking independence from Serbia and may succeed if Serbia could be seen as oppressors. This motive was significantly heightened in 1999 because the Kosovo Albanians were receiving international support for their campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The record contains evidence of significant departures of Kosovo Albanians from Pristina. There is also evidence that NATO was bombing civilian structures in Pristina. Witnesses Marinkovic and Filipovic testified about NATO bombing of civilian structures in Pristina. The Trial Chamber rejected their testimony with the following language: "Indeed a significant number of reports made at the time are in evidence and none of them confirms Marinkovic and Filipovic's testimony that civilian buildings in Pristina were targeted." That's Volume II, paragraph 837 in some other not-true statement by the Trial Chamber. On 13 April 1999, in Exhibit P2004, a Pristina Corps combat report to the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command Staff, said this: "The following civilian targets were attacked in Pristina: Jugopetrol warehouse, the plastics factory, the bus station, and the Dardanija neighbourhood. The report also listed targets that were not classified as civilian: The Lukare warehouse and the Slatina warehouse." The Trial Chamber cited this document, but as evidence of non-confirmation of the testimony of the two witnesses, yet the document clearly supports their testimony that civilian targets were bombed. There are several additional documents reporting NATO attacks on civilian targets. Although many were cited by the Trial Chamber, it was for other reasons, and they failed to consider the civilian consequences of the NATO attacks. I refer you to 4D172; 3D280, not cited by the Trial Chamber; 5D223, not cited by the Trial Chamber; 4D286; 4D342, not cited by the Trial Chamber; 4D290; 5D225, not cited by the Trial Chamber; 5D914, and that's characterised by the Chamber as a document suggesting that buildings and objects forming part of the Serbian civilian infrastructure were bombed by NATO. But actually, what it reports is a NATO attack on a column of Albanian refugees returning to their homes on tractors, killing 100 and wounding 50. See Volume I, paragraph 1214. 4D358; 5D222, not cited by the Trial Chamber; 6D1489, not cited by the Chamber; 4D336; 5D228, not cited; 5D241, not cited; 5D242, not cited; 4D309, which the Trial Chamber says shows forcible displacement and it does not, Volume III, paragraph 848. So did General Pavkovic in all of his efforts to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law do anything for the protection of these Kosovo Albanian civilians? And the answer is yes. In early April, right after the bombing started, Pavkovic phoned General Branko Krga, chief of legal administration in the Supreme Command Staff, by telephone with regard to the Kosovo Albanian refugees, expressing his concern that arrangements were needed to be made to take care of these people, make sure they were clothed and housed and fed and things of that nature, and what do they recommend that he do about that. That's transcript 16916. Pavkovic issued several orders for the protection of civilians during the NATO bombing period. Shortly after his conversation with General Krga, his Grom 4 order of 10 April 1999, which is 4D308, was issued. It contains specific instructions for civilian protection. In item 2, paragraph 5, page 4, he orders 3rd Army units at: "Established axes on the state border, organise the reception of refugees, and offer help to governing organs in their further care." The last sentence of item 4, page 6 reads: "Carry out the defensive operation in two stages with full application of and honouring the Geneva Conventions on the protection of victims of war and its Additional Protocols." 4D212, not cited by the Trial Chamber, a 14 April 1999 document, first of all, indicates that the Pavkovic orders from 10 April regarding civilians are being honoured. This is a report by a commission he appointed to look into the situation of refugees being accommodated in Istok. While the commission found that none had been accommodated there, there were 544 that had been in a school in Suvi Lukavac, which I think is nearby. After receiving food and fuel from the staff, these refugees travelled towards Djakovica in the direction of Albania. They were intercepted at one point by the VJ as they approached the border and were told that it was closed. They were given food and sent back Istok. He reported that the VJ had treated them properly. P1306 of 16 April 1999 is a further example that Pavkovic's orders in this regard were being implemented. The preamble reads: "Due to the operations of the NATO air forces and the remaining terrorist forces against civilian targets, every day the civilian population in the corps zone is exposed to direct attacks which seriously threatens its safety." The document then sets out very specific orders for the care of the civilian population. Pristina Corps commander Lazarevic issued this very specific order to his subordinate units and indicated that he would personally bring to account anyone who would violate the order. The Trial Chamber, however, used this document only to show that Lazarevic was aware of the massive displacement of the population. See Volume III, paragraph 851. They did report the protection language in paragraph 902, however. Exhibit 4D350, 19 April 1999, is another very strong order from Pavkovic to the units commanded by him regarding the treatment of the Albanian civilian population. It required accommodation, food, medical care. It required the designation of safe villages where they could be accommodated. The order says: "Monitor the movements of the civilian population in your zones of responsibility daily and ensure they have the necessary protection and can return to their homes or to sectors outside the combat operation zones." In paragraph 720 of Volume III, the Trial Chamber mentioned that it was clear that Pavkovic was aware of the confiscation of identity documents based on his OTP interview. He also said in the interview that he established that no VJ personnel were involved and that he sent a report about it to the Supreme Command Staff. And in this document, 4D350 in paragraph 5, he clearly prevented the VJ from doing so. The paragraph reads: "Use vigorous measures to prevent personal items and private property being taken from the refugee population. Take measures to prosecute violators." This order was transmitted down the chain of command as can be seen from the following: 5D201, 19 April; 5D1033, 20 April; 5D1004, 20 April, all from lower units under his authority. And it's clear that they were being implemented. With regard to these efforts, the Chamber in Volume III, paragraph 765 made this conclusion: "Noting the statement relating to the security situation in Kosovo to prepare these actions and mask our actions with undertakings for civilians made by Minic in Pavkovic's presence at a Joint Command meeting in August 1998 at P1468, pages 52 to 53, and noting K90's evidence that Kosovo Albanians were prevented from leaving areas in which the VJ was operating because that would have left the VJ without the protection of surrounding civilians and thus vulnerable to NATO attacks, T 9408, the Chamber does not consider these to be genuine measures to limit the criminal offending occurring in Kosovo." With respect, I must say that this makes no sense. The reference to a statement by Minic eight months earlier in a Joint Command meeting being somehow related to the events of April 1999, if you look at what Minic said in P1468, it's impossible to tell what he's talking about. It has something to do with a media report about something going on in Junik. It's an absolutely amazing jump to suggest that he's looking forward to April of 1999 when he makes that remark and that Pavkovic understood it as such. Second, to suggest that the order and similar orders at the time were not genuine is also ridiculous. These orders went from Pavkovic to all units under his command, from Lazarevic to all units under his command. To suggest that they were not genuine, it would be necessary for there to be some evidence that there was then a communication that these orders were to be ignored. They were top secret orders, they were confidential orders, they weren't public. There is not one shred of such evidence, that they should be ignored. These documents probably only became public for the first time at this Tribunal. There's certainly no evidence they were public when issued. So what we have are two competing reasonable conclusions or may be reasonable conclusions. A reasonable Trial Chamber must adopt that consistent with innocence and this Trial Chamber did not. In Volume III, paragraph 1172, the Chamber went beyond the confines of the indictment and emphasised evidence of violence and intimidation in other locations based on the testimony of three former VJ members, K90, K73, and K54. K90 described how his unit expelled the Kosovo Albanians from their homes during the NATO campaign. K90's written statement was admitted into evidence. The statement was written in English and this is an important thing to be understood, the way these statements were taken. They would interview the witness and the statement would be written down in English and typed up and printed out in English, and then they would -- an interpreter would read that statement to the witness and the witness would then be asked to sign it. That's what happened with K90's written statement. But he said in court that he wasn't quite sure it was read back to him. That's at T 9309. As to its language talking about expelling villagers, he said in his testimony in court that the word "expulsion" in his statement was not a correct translation. He said villagers were relocated basically for their own safety. That's at T 9298. The Trial Court really failed to clarify that this witness contended that his written statement was not correct. He gave his testimony in court, under oath, subject to cross-examination. Such testimony should always be superior to a questionable written statement. K90 in his testimony in court said this: "I can guarantee that nobody could or was allowed to take anything with them throughout the war in Kosovo. In my unit, I don't know about the other units, but in the unit where I served, nobody was allowed to touch anything that belonged to somebody else. People that were caught doing that were prosecuted and ended up in prison." That's T 9303. K73, transcript 3324, describes helping an elderly Albanian couple. He says: "Quite simply, we respected these people and tried to help them in every conceivable way to do something for them." Now, for some reason, at that point as he made that statement, Judge Bonomy interrupted the testimony and said: "... exploration of rather immaterial events, Mr. Hannis, please." And then Hannis says to the witness: "Okay, let me stop you there." At transcript 3367 the witness says: "I never shot at civilians, at women, at children. That goes against the grain of all military principles in the Army of Yugoslavia and of my unit. We never did that. I swear, I always told my soldiers, my subordinates, 'If I ever hear that any one of you, even if I hear of such a thing, I don't even have to see it, that any one of you kills civilians, raped women, or did such obnoxious things, I'm going to be your prosecutor and executioner.' "I assert before this Court that my unit never committed crimes, counsel ..." T 3380 and 81, K-73 says the reason for the removal action was that KLA were in civilian clothing, hiding among the Albanian civilians, that they were to send them to Korenica, they were ordered to send them to Korenica where the police could check them against lists of KLA members. He agrees that there was a military reason for this action, to try to locate KLA soldiers and remove them as combatants from among the civilian population. So these people actually were sent to Korenica and something pretty horrible happened there, many of them were killed. The witness and his unit was later assigned with Lazarevic as body-guards. He said during the time he was assigned as a body-guard to Lazarevic in Pristina he never saw Pavkovic, didn't see him anywhere. That's T 3392. There's controversy about a Pavkovic speech where he was alleged to have said: We need to clean our backs of Albanians. This witness says what that meant was to clean our backs of the KLA and break down or break up their units and incapacitate them in order for us to be able to fight NATO without having to worry about them being behind our backs. At that time they were expecting a land invasion by NATO and they couldn't face that land invasion if KLA was also behind them and they were basically surrounded by troops and that makes sense. K54 did say that Albanians were expelled from Petrovo Selo, the purpose was not clear, and he definitely did not say that they left Kosovo or were forced to leave Kosovo. With the bombing nearby they may have been relocated for their safety. It's simply not clear, and no Court should conclude beyond reasonable that he's talking about forced expulsions in accordance with the alleged JCE plan. I've got more information here about arming and disarming, but I think we've talked about that enough and I'm going to skip that. I want to go to some more about the breaches of the October Agreements. This is ground three of our appeal. It's discussed by the Trial Chamber in Volume III, paragraph 685 through 690 under the heading "Breaches of the October Agreements." The claim is that Pavkovic breached the October Agreements by bringing VJ units into Kosovo. This claim is simply not true, it's not supported by any evidence. The context of the actual breaches is this: Due to the restrictions on the VJ imposed by the October Agreements, the KLA was able to largely rebuild itself and reoccupy many areas that had been abandoned. As 1999 began, the threat of NATO intervention increased. The Rambouillet conference was organised and the success of the peace process diminished. The FRY began filling a need to prepare for an invasion. Thus, there was a need to restore troop strength to Kosovo where KLA had been building. This was not a Pavkovic programme but one activated at the highest levels of the FRY government. On January 16 1999, General Ojdanic issued Grom 3, his directive based on the projected introduction by force of a multi-national NATO brigade into Kosovo. It envisioned the additional build-up of VJ forces in Kosovo which had recently begun. It assigned specific responsibilities to the 3rd Army in that regard. It's an important document to achieve an understanding of the alleged breaches. It's 3D690. I would refer Your Honours to 3D557 at page 7, that's a 3 December 1998 document in which Dimitrijevic tells the collegium that the KLA has not been restricted and are rebuilding and are a future threat. 3D1025 of 6 December 1998, Dimitrijevic receives a security organ report on KLA build-up in the Podujevo area. 3D1036 of 26 December, Dimitrijevic receives a security organ report that KLA has trenches and bunkers along the road near Podujevo and are firing on the VJ moving along that road. P928, 24 December collegium meeting, Dimitrijevic says this: "The increasing number of terrorist acts against Serbs is a special danger at the moment, as the intent is to intimidate them and encourage them to move out of Kosovo and Metohija as well as to bring terrorist activities into urban areas." At this moment this occurs most frequently in the area of Podujevo, where the Serbian villages of Obrandza, Pirane, and Velika Reka have been almost completely abandoned. P936, 14 January 1999, another collegium meeting, Kosovac lists units relocated from peace-time garrisons to Kosovo and subordinated to the Pristina Corps. These units were sent pursuant to a special order by General Ojdanic, Pavkovic not involved. Dimitrijevic, on page 11, proposes that additional forces may be necessary in Kosovo to deal with the terrorist threat. Volume III, paragraph 689, the Chamber says: "In early 1999, Pavkovic brought a number of units into Kosovo to augment the forces of the VJ."
