The sentence has no cite at all but is probably covered by the remainder of the paragraph where this is said: "Pavkovic brought the 72nd Special Brigade into the interior of Kosovo prior to 25 February 1999 despite an instruction from Ojdanic to keep it in the border belt area." This is covered well and completely in our brief beginning at paragraph 164. I'd only add the following. Exhibit P1948 is the Ojdanic order regarding this unit. You'll see in paragraph 1 of that order that the purpose for it being subordinated to the 3rd Army command was - these are Ojdanic's words - "carrying out anti-terrorist and anti-sabotage tasks." These are tasks that could only be carried out in Kosovo. So clearly this was an order that that 72nd Brigade be sent to Kosovo. Nothing in this order says anything about it being kept at the border and kept out of Kosovo. P941, a collegium meeting, Ojdanic says at page 24 that he disagreed with the proposal for the 72nd Military Police Battalion to be deployed to Kosovo, but he signed the order doing it. So why does he say at a collegium meeting he disagreed with it? And then he says he ordered that it should be deployed at the edges of Kosovo; that's also not true, he didn't order that. He's now distressed to learn that they've been transferred to Kosovo and split up. He says this only after Dimitrijevic complains that the units should not have been moved without his having being consulted. That's page 16. It's important to know that Ojdanic did absolutely nothing after he said he ordered that it be kept at the border, he did absolutely nothing to bring it back out of Kosovo. He and Dimitrijevic both knew that it was operating inside Kosovo and that's clear by a security organ report of 2 March 1999 reporting a successful mission having been carried out by this unit. We'll never know what Ojdanic was doing in this meeting and why he was saying the things he was saying because it's totally contrary to his orders. Pavkovic says in his interview at P1319 -- or he did not say that he brought additional troops into Kosovo. He said the VJ did that and that's a true statement. It was ordered and organised at the highest level. The evidence is clear. It is not something that he could do on his own. Then on 6 March 1999, the Supreme Command Staff, Ojdanic, ordered the transfer of the 37th Motorised Brigade from the 2nd Army to the 3rd Army "due to the threat to the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the zone of the Pristina Corps, in order to provide appropriate forces for implementation of tasks of the 3rd Army, and pursuant to Articles 5 and 6 of the Law on the Yugoslav Army." 5D261, 13 March 1999, the General Staff in an order signed by deputy chief General Marjanovic ordered mobilisation and/or partial mobilisation of a number of units, ordering their resubordination. The 252nd Armoured Brigade from the 1st Army to the 3rd Army. The Mechanised Battalion of the 211th was sent from Kursumlijska Banja to Malo Kosovo which is near Podujevo. In 3D683, not cited by the Trial Chamber, 16 March of 1999, the General Staff by Marjanovic again ordered the 72nd Special Brigade Reconnaissance and Sabotage Battalion subordinated to the 3rd Army. No request by Pavkovic is shown in the preamble or in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, I wonder whether it's the right time for us to stop. I'll give you ten more minutes after we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a 30-minute break. We'll resume at ten minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to conclude very briefly with the subject --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have counsel's text. Kindly speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, interpreters. Conclude very quickly with this. There is simply no evidence, testimony or otherwise, that would support the conclusion that Pavkovic brought VJ units into Kosovo in violation of the October Agreements. The General Staff ordered all additions to VJ forces in Kosovo. On two or three instances these were at the request of Pavkovic, but it remains that all transfers to Kosovo were on Supreme Command Staff orders not 3rd Army orders. No reasonable Trial Chamber could reach the conclusion that the Trial Chamber made in this regard. Now, Your Honours, for the little bit of time that's left, I want to move to one of my pet-peeve documents. This is P1439, and this document was heavily relied on by the Prosecutor and by the Trial Chamber to establish that Pavkovic was violating orders of his superior, Samardzic. On 5 October of 1998, Pavkovic sent a document to Samardzic and the Trial Chamber misinterpreted its meaning partly due to translation difficulties and partly due to ignoring very important testimony. Paragraph 2 speaks of the plan authorised by the president that envisioned the formation of rapid intervention forces. Pavkovic then says that he telephones Samardzic on return from a Joint Command meeting on 19 and 20 September and informed him of a Joint Command decision to form rapid intervention forces. He then sent that decision to Samardzic, which Samardzic rejected in his order 168-262 of 3 October. Because of the need to carry forward with the plan as set out in paragraph 2 and the denial of the formation of rapid intervention forces, he is now asking the 3rd Army command to determine the composition of forces to carry out the plan ordered by the president without the use of rapid intervention forces. The preamble reference in this document of 5 October 1998 refers to a 3rd Army order, 168-262 of 3 October. In paragraph 1 of this document he informs Samardzic that he has not formed any new groups in violation of the order forbidding him to do so of 3 October. The matter is complicated by the fact that the 3 October order number 168-262 is not in evidence in this case. But it's clarified, however, by testimony in the case. And the controversy about this is is paragraph 1 says this: "Contrary to your orders, Pristina Corps command has not formed any new combat groups." And actually, that's a mistranslation. It should say something like: "The Pristina Corps command has not formed combat groups as you have ordered." So it wasn't violating any kind of an order and that becomes clear. On October 19th, the witness Radinovic is being questioned by Judge Bonomy regarding this document. It's clear that Judge Bonomy believes because of the English translation that it shows that Pavkovic has violated a Samardzic order, and Radinovic has trouble understanding the question because he's looking at the B/C/S version of the document. So he sees something different. Bonomy refers him -- Judge Bonomy refers him to paragraph 1 and the language contrary to your orders. Then he refers him to the second paragraph, under number 2, where Pavkovic points out that he calls Samardzic after the JC meeting to inform him of the decision to establish rapid deployment forces. And Bonomy then asks him how he reads this situation. Radinovic says that the document indicates the commander did not allow the establishment of the rapid deployment force. And then the Judge asks: "But does it not look as though General Pavkovic just went ahead and did it?" Radinovic says: "Well, he probably proposed that because the combat groups that had been established earlier were engaged in other tasks and there would be a need to intervene and there aren't any appropriate forces for that, hence his request to have that kind of force created." That's T 17340 and 341. So Radinovic clearly sees this document as a request to create some kind of force to replace the combat groups that had been denied. Much earlier in the trial, Prosecutor Hannis brought this document, P1439, to the attention of Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Hannis also believed it to be evidence that Pavkovic had disobeyed a Samardzic order. Vasiljevic's testimony is even clearer. Again, Vasiljevic is looking at a B/C/S version of this document. Prosecutor Hannis showed him the language from paragraph 1, saying, "Contrary to your orders the Pristina Corps has not formed any new combat groups," and then asks him this: "Under what circumstances was it permissible for a subordinate to disobey an order of a superior commander?" Vasiljevic answers that properly regarding the constitution and the laws and then says: "Now, what is this here? I don't think there's any controversy here. It was just stated that the Pristina Corps had not formed these new combat groups yet." He is then referred to language under paragraph 2 and asked what this says about the relative relations between the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and the Joint Command, and Vasiljevic answers: "I think that the commander of the 3rd Army still has jurisdiction over the command of the Pristina Corps. And if you read this, the first paragraph, it says here that the Pristina Corps did not form combat groups in contravention of your order, and the order actually forbade the establishment, the formation, of such groups. They were not formed and this was not in contravention; in other words, the order was complied with." At that point the Prosecutor went on to other matters. That's T 9093 to 95. The Prosecution did not even argue in their final brief before the Trial Court that this document showed Pavkovic disobeying a Samardzic order. The two military witnesses had made it so clear that the document was being misread. In response to our supplementary brief we had an annex attached that showed a huge number of villages that were outside the border belt that are in various orders and reports during a time when it was being contended that the VJ was not operating outside the border belt properly. And the Prosecution challenged that annex that we didn't cite that there was any evidence for it. The evidence, Your Honours, is 4D381, it's a map. It's a big map, and it's easy to find all of those villages outside the border belt on that map. I think my time has virtually expired and I simply want to say to you that I have another hour or so that I would like to tell you about some other things and I don't have time to do that, and I think they're important things that you should know but I haven't got time to do it. Maybe I will get to some of them a little later. What I would really like to emphasise based upon the things I've told you this morning is that you've got to be very careful about accepting the pronouncements of the Trial Chamber without looking behind them to see what -- where the evidence is or if there is any. And I've shown you several examples today where there is none behind those pronouncements and I could show you several more, and within five minutes or so I could probably find another one, that quickly, because all you have to do is look at the pronouncement, look at the citation and you'll find that it is not what it is said to be. So I hope you will pay that kind of attention to the evidence in this case because the evidence is what's important, not what the Trial Chamber said. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Judge Guney has a question. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Guney has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, as you know, on the 21st July 1998, a plan comprising both military and political measures for suppression and combatting terrorism was adopted. What were the measures, immediate and important measures, taken following this plan which was approved in the Milosevic residence in Belgrade? Could you please enlighten us on this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a very important document, Your Honour, and you've hit on one that's very important to this case. The Prosecution was contending throughout the Prosecution case that the VJ was being used outside the border belt in Kosovo mainly by Pavkovic without orders bypassing the chain of command, and that that was improper and illegal and that it couldn't be done. And it came as a significant surprise to the Prosecution when we brought this document, that's 4D139, to the attention of a witness in the case, and then 4D140, which was the 3rd Army version of that order, and it was -- 4D137, I'm just told is what it is. In any event, it authorised and ordered by Perisic who just four or five days before had told Milosevic the VJ shouldn't be used outside the border belt because it was illegal, nobody was ever able to show us any law that made it illegal and still haven't been able to, but that was Perisic's claim. Anyhow, this order ordered the use of the VJ outside the border belt. The order was then -- became a 3rd Army order that ordered immediate use of the VJ outside the border belt. And finally, that became a matter that even the Trial Chamber agreed authorised the use of the VJ outside the border belt as of 21 July. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge T, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, maybe this belongs to the hour that you don't have, but you were approaching the issue of an agreement and in your appeal brief you contend that the Trial Chamber erred with regard to the existence of JCE since there should have been, and I quote, paragraph 25, "a real plan emanating from real agreement." And your brief continues: "It does not materialise out of thin air or out of events on the ground. There must be an agreement." Could you please elaborate on your -- upon this argument and explain what you mean by the "real agreement." Of course if you look into the jurisprudence of the Tribunals, you would find a suggestion that a common purpose does not require a specific and formal agreement with all the seals and fancy bands. But at the same time, if you look at the jurisprudence, you would find that there should exist an understanding, an arrangement, that might be amounting to an agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a long answer and a short answer. I'll try the short answer and if you want more, I can do that. The problem is this: By taking a set of facts and trying to take those facts and find just because of the way they relate to each other that there must have been some kind of an agreement and, therefore, there was a JCE is kind of a dangerous road to go down and a difficult road to go down. Because you have to prove things beyond a reasonable doubt in a criminal court. And even if the law, as it says, that it can arise out of the situation, it still -- you still have to have the group that's part of the JCE having an agreement among themselves as to what the purpose of that is and assisting each other in that process. So even though there does -- there's no formal agreement, there's no written document or anything like that, there has to be some kind of communication between them about this is the goal that we're going to pursue and we're going to do it together. And that's what's missing from the evidence in this case, is no indication that there was anything like that. There are hundreds of pages of meetings of the collegium of the General Staff, hundreds of pages of documents at that very, very high level and never in any of those documents is there any, any, discussion of a plan to expel Kosovo Albanians for the reasons suggested. And so what I'm saying is that without some evidence that these people had a plan that they were working together on that would outweigh beyond a reasonable doubt that it happened in a different manner, it doesn't prove a JCE. Does that answer you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: So was this a long answer or a short answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: I would need a shorter answer to what the real agreement is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well I don't think there is a real agreement. I don't think there was any agreement at all. This was a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just looking for a definition from Ackerman what the real agreement is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh. The real agreement is that there is some evidence showing that everybody that is a member of the joint criminal enterprise had the same goal in mind, they agreed with each other about what they were doing; that's the real agreement. If that's not there, there's no JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Pocar has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Following on your answer, Mr. Ackerman, are you -- I want to try to understand your point. Are you suggesting that the agreement to be real cannot be proved by circumstantial evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it can, but circumstantial evidence is pretty tricky. It has to outweigh anything else. And again, we're back at beyond a reasonable doubt thing. But yes, you don't have to have a written agreement. That's what the Tribunal says. I don't have to agree with the law that has been established in this Tribunal, but the law is that it can arise without any proof of an actual written agreement or a sit down and discuss kind of agreement that is recorded in any way, so yes, it can arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think it's time to hear the response from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might just have a moment to set up and get ready. If I might have just one more moment. We'll need just a moment, Your Honour, to distribute some charts I've prepared for today to help with the -- my submission. So if I could just wait a moment to have those distributed to everyone in the courtroom so they can follow along. Hopefully you'll find them helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand that this is just for the help for your presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is not evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: It is not evidence, it is not part of the record. It is merely a list of particular findings by the Trial Chamber I'll be referring to during the course of my submission, but of course, as you correctly point out, we would not call this evidence in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, General Pavkovic was a key member of the joint criminal enterprise. As 3rd Army commander in 1999, he ordered his troops into joint operations with the MUP throughout Kosovo with the intent that they engage in a campaign of terror and violence to drive out Kosovo Albanians. These operations resulted in murders, sexual assaults, and the displacement of over 700.000 Kosovo Albanians. He covered up his subordinates' crimes or else took no meaningful steps in response, thereby creating an atmosphere where perpetrators felt they could and did get away with further crimes. The Trial Chamber reasonably found, based on this and other evidence, that Pavkovic shared the intent of his fellow JCE members, Nikola Sainovic and Sreten Lukic, and that Pavkovic made a significant contribution to the common criminal plan. Our submissions today will focus on these two points. Specifically, I will discuss Pavkovic's mens rea and I will answer Your Honours' questions relating to JCE I and JCE 3 as they relate to Pavkovic. My colleague Mr. Menon will then address Your Honours' question on the actus reus as it relates to Pavkovic. As a preliminary matter, we would note that today counsel for Pavkovic has misconstrued the standard for review on appeal. He has broadly repeated trial submissions rather than, as he should have, demonstrating that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached the factual finding in question based on the totality of the evidence. For example, he today has highlighted certain exhibits, isolated exhibits, that are favourable to his position without addressing or rebutting contrary Trial Chamber findings. A good example of this would be his discussion of the ineffective measures that Trial Chamber took Pavkovic took. Another example is a failure to read the trial judgement as a whole. An example of this would be the earlier discussion today of the witness K90. The Trial Chamber was well aware that there was a change, difference, I'll say, between K90's written statement where he used the word "expelled," and his oral testimony where he discussed -- he explained it was "relocated." The Trial Chamber specifically discussed this relevant point at Volume II, paragraph 74, and further explained why it was reasonable to rely on K90 as a credible witness on this point and others. Because today we're only addressing these two points on mens rea and actus reus, we won't go into his challenges regarding the existence of the common purpose. We would rely on Mr. Kremer's submissions in that regard from yesterday, and that's in the appeals transcript at page 217 to 232, and is also dealt with in our response brief to Pavkovic, paragraphs 15 to 28. At this time, Your Honours, I'd like to turn to Pavkovic's shared intent for the JCE, and the first -- by doing so, I will address what we have numbered as question ten in Your Honours' addendum, which I'll read so there is no confusion. "Discuss, as a legal matter as well as with respect to the particular Trial Chamber's findings for each appellant convicted of JCE I, whether the actus reus and mens rea of a JCE member may be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose of the JCE." I'm going to talk now about the mens rea part of this question. My colleague Mr. Menon will subsequently discuss the actus reus. Yesterday Ms. Martin Salgado for the Prosecution set out our position on the law for this question. As she clarified, we understand Your Honours to be further asking whether each JCE accused was found to have shared the intent for the JCE prior to the existence of the common purpose. The short answer for Pavkovic is no. The Trial Chamber found that Pavkovic shared the intent for the JCE based on a wide range of evidence arising during the 1999 conflict, during the time the crimes were committed. For example, Pavkovic ordered on May 7th, 1999, that his troops control the movements of Kosovo Albanian civilians. And that's at judgement Volume III, paragraph 736. Furthermore, during the 1999 conflict, Pavkovic did nothing in the face of massive forcible displacement and crimes of violence or else covered up crimes. He bypassed the chain of command to work with Milosevic on the issue of Kosovo. In addition to this evidence from 1999, the Trial Chamber also looked at other evidence that revealed the pattern of Pavkovic's behaviour. For example, Pavkovic covered up crimes in 1998, just as he would do in 1999. He violated the chain of command to work directly with Milosevic in 1998, just as he would do in 1999. As the Trial Chamber said in Volume III, paragraph 665, he advanced his aggressive strategy of using the VJ and MUP together in Kosovo in 1998, just as he would do - as other Trial Chamber's findings show - in 1999. The Trial Chamber properly examined the totality of Pavkovic's conduct, the pattern of this conduct through 1998 and 1999, when finding he shared the intent for the JCE I crimes. We heard earlier today the assertion from the counsel for Pavkovic that the 1998 evidence was irrelevant. I plan to show otherwise. At this point, though, before we get to 1998, I'm going to focus a bit more on the 1999 conflict and the Trial Chamber's focus on evidence relating to Pavkovic from this time period. A good starting point is our first slide. This is the order I've just mentioned from May 7th, 1999, in the midst of the conflict, from Pavkovic to his troops to control the movement of the Kosovo Albanians. This is particular -- this document as a whole is a comprehensive list -- I'm just pausing to make sure that everyone is seeing the slide.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters for my speed. My understanding is we all have the slide in front of us. Explaining yet again, this is a list of instructions to Pavkovic's troops. Among various logistical and strategic goals, he adds the following: "Ensure complete control of the territory and movement of Siptar civilians in your zones of responsibility." "Siptar" means Kosovo Albanians. Your Honours, this is what the JCE boils down to, ensure control of Kosovo by ensuring control of the movement of the Kosovo Albanian civilians. It's as simple as that. The Trial Chamber reasonably, properly, focused on the discriminatory nature of this order because it does not say "civilians," but makes a point to say "Siptar civilians." In line with this is our next slide. This is a report from Pavkovic a few days later noting an attack by his troops on a village and the resulting displacement of civilians. As you see in the highlighted portion: "A part of the units of the 7th Infantry Brigade and Pec Military Detachment in an operation of routing the Siptar terrorist forces in the sector ..." And then it lists various villages. And then we go to the end: "... and about 10.000 civilians from that sector were sent towards Klina and Pec." As the Trial Chamber noted, there's no reference to NATO bombing at the time of this report, Volume III, paragraph 736, which is Pavkovic's usual explanation for the flight of civilians. Rather, this report is a straightforward account of how the VJ troops forced Kosovo Albanian civilians out of their villages. My next point, Your Honours, is that this May 7th order and May 10th report are not isolated examples. What they do is make explicit what had already been happening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge T has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: To return to my submissions, Your Honour, this report that we've just looked at a bit more in detail and the May 7th order are making explicit what has already been happening since March 1999, the mass forcible displacement and the other violent crimes which Pavkovic was well informed of and could see for himself from the ground in Pristina. So now I'm going to turn to Pavkovic's awareness during the 1999 conflict of the crimes of his troops and the MUP. We agree with counsel for Pavkovic that: "He could only be expected to deal with what he knew about specifically at the time ..." and that's from the appeal brief for the Defence at paragraph 196. Well, let's look now at what he did know about specifically at the time. And now I would turn to the chart we've had distributed and you'll see there's two years, 1998/1999. I'll be focusing on the 1999 chart. I'll just pause and make sure everyone has a copy. Your Honour, this is a table listing the Trial Chamber's findings of the examples it focused on in relation to Pavkovic as to his awareness of VJ and MUP crimes in 1999. These are orders and reports that were received by Pavkovic or received -- received by him or issued from him or meetings that he attended. For purposes of clarity, I've highlighted in bold those that deal with forcible displacement. I'm just pausing to make sure everyone is following the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. We've heard today, actually, a few challenges to some specific examples on this chart, but really, the important point for my -- the important point is the sheer volume of examples that Pavkovic was aware of the crimes of his subordinates and [Realtime transcript read in error "in"] the MUP, starting from the very beginning in March 1999 and reaching all the way through the end, including the indictment itself, which is of course Your Honour's question I will be addressing later. Apart from these specific examples, Pavkovic admitted that he knew identification documents were being taken from Kosovo Albanians at the border. That's at Volume III, paragraph 720. Pavkovic knew of illegal takings and distribution of Kosovo Albanian property by the VJ and military justice system in Volume III, paragraph 764. Moreover, in 1999, Pavkovic was in Kosovo more than 95 per cent of the time and present in Pristina when thousands were being forcibly displaced. That's at Volume III, paragraph 716 to 717. And as the Trial Chamber's findings in Volume II, at paragraphs 838 and following, make clear, these displacements went from March through May 1999. Having looked at the sheer volume of information of crimes of which Pavkovic became aware of, I'd like to turn to my next point: What did he do in response? He lied about his ability to hold perpetrators accountable. That's at Volume III, paragraph 757. He took ineffective measures. What does he not do? He takes no meaningful steps to hold them accountable, Volume III, paragraph 777, and he never refuses to order the VJ in the joint operations with the MUP, Volume III, paragraph 780. What Pavkovic did not do given this awareness of the crimes in 1999 sheds light on his shared intent as the Trial Chamber reasonably found. But there's one other thing Pavkovic did in response to some of these crimes, the cover-ups. Pavkovic has argued in his appeal brief at paragraph 223 that: "The integral element of committing a crime is usually covering up the evidence of that crime." We couldn't agree more. What, then, are we to make of the fact that Pavkovic himself underreported crimes in 1999 during the campaign of terror and violence to drive out the Kosovo Albanians, paragraph [sic] 3, 776. And after first being caught in May 1999, he went ahead and did it again in June 1999. And that's Volume III, paragraph 737, 752, and 752 [sic]. Finally on this point of the cover-ups, it's important to note that the two meetings in Belgrade on May 16th and 17th, 1999, to discuss the crimes in Kosovo were the result of Pavkovic having been caught underreporting crimes, Volume III, paragraphs 738 to 740. So at this May 17th meeting with fellow JCE members Sainovic and Milosevic and other people present at the meeting, when Pavkovic proposes a commission to investigate, it is only possible because he'd already been caught in his cover-up. In any event, he never followed up on this idea for a commission, Volume III, paragraph 740. The final point I'd like to address from 1999, during the time the crimes were being committed, is Pavkovic's bypassing the chain of command. He violated the chain of command so he could work directly with Milosevic on the issue of Kosovo. For example, an example that's been referred to earlier today, in April 1999 when Pavkovic and Milosevic planned an action together, it was left to Ojdanic, his superior, to offer only suggestions about the proposed action, Volume III, paragraphs 503, 534, and 705. We've heard today what counsel for Pavkovic believes to have occurred during this particular incident. His interpretation of the evidence and speculation does not rebut the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding based on the evidence it cited. Another example of this 1999 bypassing the chain of command came in mid-June 1999 when Pavkovic was seen leaving Milosevic's office, Volume III, paragraph 708. And Ojdanic commented that Pavkovic placed more importance on keeping Sainovic informed than Ojdanic informed, Volume III, paragraph 361. Now that we've looked at this evidence from 1999 from the conflict, let's turn to the other evidence that the Trial Chamber examined which demonstrated the pattern of Pavkovic's behaviour, and let's start where we left off. This is bypassing the chain of command in 1998 to work directly with Milosevic, just as he would do in 1999. The Trial Chamber made extensive findings on this topic at Volume III, paragraphs 642, 665. We've heard some again isolated challenges today that do not address the totality of these findings and the evidence cited therein. But rather than go into that, I'm going to focus on why Pavkovic was well suited to work closely with Milosevic on the issue of Kosovo, and to do so, we'll turn to our next slide. This is a letter from Pavkovic to the 3rd Army command on July 23rd, 1998, cited at Volume III, paragraph 652 of the judgement. Recall that at this time Pavkovic is Pristina Corps commander and not 3rd Army commander as he will later become. As he says in the highlighted excerpts: "If urgent measures are not taken, Kosovo will be lost forever ..." "I cannot resign myself to the fact that as a soldier" -- I'm sorry, I'm at the -- that was obviously the first highlighted excerpt and then I'll just start reading towards the bottom in the second excerpt. "... I cannot resign myself to the fact that as a soldier I have not done everything I was required to do in order to avoid such a situation," in other words, avoid the loss of Kosovo. The Trial Chamber noted at Volume III, paragraph 765, that this letter demonstrated Pavkovic's determination to keep Kosovo which led him to go beyond his normal duties, to do whatever it took. It's not a coincidence that just two days before this letter, Pavkovic had been promoted to lieutenant-general, Volume III, paragraph 649. And by the end of the same year, 1998, Perisic and Samardzic who opposed Milosevic's approach to Kosovo were out and Pavkovic had been promoted again. I'd like to turn briefly to two other examples of Pavkovic's approach as evidenced by his letter of his -- what he was willing to do to keep control of Kosovo. The first example is the arming and disarming of Albanians and non-Albanians. What the Trial Chamber found helped show the shared intent, Volume III, 779. Pavkovic was fully aware of the simmering ethnic tensions between non-Albanians and Albanians. As the Trial Chamber summarised Pavkovic's own words, Volume III, paragraph 669, he stated that it is known from the previous historical period that it - and the Trial Chamber explained this meant the conflict between the Albanian and non-Albanian population - took place every time that events of this kind happened in Kosovo and that crimes occurred when there were such conflicts and people were protecting their villages. As the Trial Chamber further held, despite this incendiary situation, as the Trial Chamber described it, Pavkovic provided weapons to the non-Albanian population while concurrently disarming the Kosovo Albanian population. Again Volume III, paragraph 669. The other example in line with Pavkovic's approach from the July 23rd letter is how he violated Ojdanic's order by moving the 72nd Special Brigade in Kosovo's interior in early 1999, which the Trial Chamber found help showed his shared intent. That's at Volume III, paragraph 778. And the findings on the moving of the brigade can be found at Volume III, 689 to 690. Pavkovic also moved his troops into Kosovo in violation of the international agreements so they would be well placed for operations in March 1999. That's at Volume III, paragraph 690. He misled others in the VJ as to aggressive approach in Kosovo by claiming that Pristina Corps and 3rd Army actions in Kosovo were defensive only, were responses to attacks. In fact, these had been preplanned by the army itself. Volume III, paragraphs 515 to 516, 546, 599, and 688. So let's move away from these examples of Pavkovic's approach to Kosovo and turn to a topic we've talked about before which goes again into the pattern of his conduct, his awareness of crimes in 1999 - and now, of course, we're talking about 1998 - by the VJ and the MUP. Pavkovic has argued in ground seven of his brief that he was not aware of crimes in 1998. The chart I passed out would say otherwise, and I would invite Your Honours to flip the page to the 1998. Again, as I mentioned before, these reflect Trial Chamber -- these reflect what the Trial Chamber focused on in relation to Pavkovic regarding his awareness in 1998 of these crimes and are orders and reports received by Pavkovic or issued from him or meetings he attended. Again, I've highlighted in bold those that deal with forcible displacement. Apart from the specific incidents on this time-line, Pavkovic admitted that VJ members had committed arson in 1998, Volume III, paragraph 672, and Pavkovic himself ordered VJ troops in the Drenica in August 1998 contrary to superior orders, excessive force was used there, and this resulted in displacement of Kosovo Albanians. Volume III, paragraphs 658 and 774, as well as Volume I, paragraphs 894, 915, 919. What does all this mean? This relates to Your Honours' question about 1998 crimes and their relevance in this case. It shows that Pavkovic knew his troops in the MUP had previously been successful in expelling civilians through crimes of violence because it means he can successfully deploy them once again in a campaign of terror and violence that will result in mass expulsions. Another pattern I'd like to highlight is what Pavkovic does in response to crimes of his subordinates. He covers up. He underreports in 1998, just as he would do in 1999. For example, he downplayed reports of a massacre at Gornje Obrinje in September 1998, where a number of civilians had been killed, including women and children, in the course of a VJ and MUP operation. Volume III, paragraphs 675 and 678; Volume I, paragraph 912. He passed on an order on July 7th, 1998, to avoid firing when internationals are present, which the Trial Chamber noted was designed to avoid detection of VJ crimes, paragraph [sic] 3, 673 and 678. He shifted the blame in 1998 -- in September 1998 from VJ forces, accused of displacement of civilians. Volume III, paragraph 674. Working backwards now, we have Pavkovic's call to arms in July 1998 to do whatever it takes. He's laying the groundwork up until March 1999, in preparation for a massive campaign of displacement. Then, after the campaign of terror and violence begins, he issues an order to keep the Kosovo Albanians moving. He does nothing in the face of forcible displacement or crimes of violence or else covers up the crimes. So we have evidence from the 1999 conflict, from the time the crimes were being committed, that is consistent with and connecting back to the 1998 evidence to show the pattern of Pavkovic's behaviour. When viewed as a whole, this evidence shows that the Trial Chamber is reasonable to find that Pavkovic shared the intent for the JCE along with Sainovic and Lukic. This concludes my answer to question ten. The next question I'm going to address is what we've numbered as your question 11: "Discuss whether and under what circumstances the mens rea under JCE I for deportation and other inhumane acts (forcible transfer) may be inferred from the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including crimes other than deportation and other inhumane acts ..." As Ms. Monchy already explained yesterday in regarding Sainovic, it was appropriate in the case of Pavkovic for the Trial Chamber to infer his shared intent based upon -- based upon, among other factors, his knowledge of the violent crimes committed in 1998 that resulted in mass displacement. Before explaining why, I want to recall for a moment the Trial Chamber's findings regarding these 1998 crimes. The Trial Chamber found that in their operations against the KLA in 1998, FRY and Serbian forces used heavy-handed tactics which forced over 200.000 civilians from their villages. Volume I, paragraph 919; and Volume III, paragraph 90. These tactics involved the burning and destruction of homes, intimidating inhabitants to move out, firing artillery shells and killing civilians. And this can be found in Volume I, between paragraphs 880 to 920. Thus, even if the Trial Chamber did not specify the departure of civilians from their homes in 1998 as forcible displacement, these departures were clearly not voluntary or lawful under international humanitarian law. As to why - turning again to Pavkovic - it is appropriate for the Trial Chamber to rely on these crimes, I'll just go back to what I mentioned earlier from the 1998 chart. It provides notice to Pavkovic of his troops and the MUP's propensity for violence. It shows that he can successfully use these same troops, again in 1999, to achieve the same results. In other words, a mass campaign of terror and violence resulting in mass expulsions. As a general matter in response to this question, we would note that an accused's knowledge of earlier crimes is simply a fact in the case and that can be relied on as other facts in this case or others. So here we have the use of the force -- Pavkovic's forces in 1999, the widespread crimes committed in 1999. All the other findings the Trial Chamber relied upon, all of which together, read as a whole, support the Trial Chamber's finding as to his shared intent. A final brief point on this. I would like to clarify for the record that yesterday Ms. Monchy, when answering a question from Judge Pocar, Your Honour, was recorded as saying "to possibly displace the Kosovo Albanians in 1999," and the transcript cite is appeal transcript page 263, line 8. Ms. Monchy actually said "forcibly displace" not "possibly displace" and we'll request a check of that. But at the very least, she meant to say "forcibly displace" and we want to avoid any confusion in that regard. That would conclude on question 11, 1998 crimes. And I'll turn to what we've numbered as your question 4: "Discuss the relevance of the indictment made public on 27 May 1999 on the mens rea of Sainovic and Pavkovic, given that the indictment was made public after the last crime for which Sainovic and Pavkovic were convicted was committed on 25 May 1999." Contrary to the argument earlier today, the Trial Chamber properly considered this indictment when assessing his shared intent. It was relevant. As the Trial Chamber said at paragraph -- Volume III, paragraph 765, his subsequent inaction is relevant to his mental state at the time. In other words, Pavkovic failing to take any effective measures during the rest of 1999 and even during 2000, when he was promoted to VJ Chief of Staff, showed that he intended the crimes in the common purpose and is in line with the pattern of his failure to take measures during the 1999 conflict itself. As to arguments today that Pavkovic was not aware of this indictment, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that he did based on the findings [indiscernible] -- and particularly note in respect to Pavkovic that he had previously received a letter directly from the ICTY Prosecutor, so this was, in fact, the second time that the ICTY Prosecutor had -- that Pavkovic had received notice from the ICTY as to crimes occurring in 1999. I'd like to turn at this point to the topic of JCE III and Your Honours' questions in that regard. First question I'm going to deal with is what we would have numbered as page number -- question 2: "Discuss, with reference to the record, whether there would be any effect on Pavkovic's appeal regarding his convictions pursuant to JCE III, if the Appeals Chamber were to accept the Prosecution's argument that the Trial Chamber applied an incorrect mens rea standard for JCE III liability." Your Honours, since the Trial Chamber found the JCE crimes of murder and persecution through murder, sexual assault, and destruction of religious property were foreseeable to Pavkovic under a higher standard than required, its finding would clearly stand under the lower possibility standard. In particular, we would note the Trial Chamber's findings on JCE III with respect to Pavkovic at paragraphs 785 to 786. Your Honours, today we heard a hypothetical from the Defence that is not this case since it assumes, contrary to the Trial Chamber's finding, that there's no common purpose and it assumes, contrary to the Trial Chamber's finding, that Pavkovic was not liable for the JCE I crimes. Finally, Your Honour, I'll turn to the other question, JCE III question, for Pavkovic which is: "Discuss, with reference to the record, whether ... the Appeals Chamber were to grant the Prosecution's argument that the sexual assaults of K62, K14, and K31 constituted persecutions, Pavkovic should be held responsible for these persecutions pursuant to JCE III." Your Honours, the answer is yes. The Trial Chamber already found Pavkovic liable under JCE III for other sexual assaults committed during the course of the JCE I crimes of deportation and forcible transfer. In fact, it found, again, him liable for these sexual assaults under a higher standard than required. With respect to the sexual assaults, the Trial Chamber focused on his awareness of the VJ and MUP's propensity for violence, and I would just note in this regard in particular the charts that I passed out from 1998 and 1999 listing these crimes of violence. The Trial Chamber also noted that the stated aim of the joint criminal enterprise was to displace people for a campaign of terror and violence, and that's at Volume III, paragraph 786. And the Trial Chamber further noted specific evidence that Pavkovic was aware of sexual assaults, Volume III, paragraph 785. The Defence has raised challenges regarding the linkage of these crimes to himself. The linkage was properly established. I would note, first as a general matter, that the Trial Chamber had found that the required link had been established between the physical perpetrators and at least one JCE member for all indicted crimes that were proven. Volume III, paragraph 468, 783, and 1132. Specifically with regard to the three sexual assaults mentioned in this question, I would read from Volume II, paragraph 889: "The Chamber ... finds it proved that three women were raped in the course of the operation to remove large numbers of Kosovo Albanians from Pristina town - K62 by three VJ or MUP personnel, K14 by a policeman, and K31 by three VJ soldiers." So his challenges based on the issue of linkage should be dismissed. As for his challenges as to whether these sexual assaults amounted to persecution, we will be addressing this in our appeal submissions on this Friday as part of the Prosecution appeal. To conclude my submissions, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that Pavkovic had the intent for the JCE I crimes and the foreseeability for the JCE III crimes. His challenges on this issue should be dismissed. And unless you have any questions, I will turn it over to my colleague or perhaps it would be our break time. I think we would certainly think a break would be appropriate subject to any questions from Your Honours.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, if I can inform you that our legal assistant, Mr. Cvijic has joined the Lazarevic team this afternoon. Thank you.
