utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As Mr. Schneider indicated, I will be discussing Pavkovic's contribution to the JCE. In doing so, I intend to answer Your Honours' question number 10 insofar as it relates to the actus reus requirement for JCE liability. As Ms. Martin Salgado clarified in her presentation yesterday, we understand the Appeals Chamber to be asking in question 10 whether each JCE accused was found to have contributed to the JCE prior to the existence of a common purpose. The short answer, Your Honours, as far as Pavkovic is concerned is no. Pavkovic's significant contribution is grounded on conduct that occurred throughout the period when the charged crimes were committed. This contribution falls into two categories. First, Pavkovic planned, ordered, and supported VJ operations in Kosovo in 1999, including by co-ordinating and planning joint VJ-MUP operations with his co-accused Sainovic and Lukic. Second, he created and sustained an environment of impunity in Kosovo through his non-measures and his concealment of crime. Your Honours, it would of course be artificial to consider Pavkovic's conduct during the 1999 campaign in a vacuum, given that in the months leading up to it, he took steps to prepare for its implementation. These preparations, which included the arming of the non-Albanian population, the disarming of the Kosovo Albanian population, and the movement of troops into Kosovo in breach of the October Agreements are also part of his contribution. They not only furthered the operations through which the charged crimes were committed, but as Mr. Kremer explained yesterday, the Trial Chamber's findings and its approach to the evidence demonstrate that the common purpose had come into existence no later than October 1998, and thus encompassed these preparatory acts. Your Honours, I want to begin by explaining how Pavkovic planned, ordered, and supported VJ operations in Kosovo. In doing so, I will explain how his introduction of troops into Kosovo in breach of the October Agreements and his involvement in the arming and disarming process furthered the operations that were carried out beginning in late March 1999. I will then turn to the environment of impunity which Pavkovic created and sustained in Kosovo during the 1999 campaign. Turning to the VJ's operations in 1999. Your Honours will recall the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 92 of Volume III that the NATO bombing was an opportunity, an opportunity for which the JCE members had been waiting to forcibly displace enough Kosovo Albanians to maintain control over Kosovo and to deal a heavy blow to the KLA. This was a campaign for which the JCE members had planned and prepared. The joint VJ-MUP operations carried out from late March 1999 through which crimes were committed were planned in the period between January and early March 1999, and this is at Volume I, paragraph 1017. The VJ's Grom 3 plan provided the basis for the VJ presence in Kosovo and its participation in joint operations with the MUP. Pavkovic issued his initial Grom 3 order on the 27th of January, 1999, further to Ojdanic's Grom 3 directive. Then, on the 1st of February, 1999, Pavkovic instructed Lazarevic to "draft a plan for blocking and destroying Albanian terrorist forces in the Drenica, Lab, and Malisevo sectors." Pavkovic also instructed that Lazarevic ensure complete co-ordination with MUP units. Lazarevic implemented Pavkovic's order through a plan which he issued on the 16th of February, 1999, and at a MUP staff meeting a day later, Lukic announced that the MUP staff had planned mopping-up operations in the same areas as those referred to in Lazarevic's plan from a day earlier. And the citations from the judgement are Volume I, paragraphs 1013 to 1015; and Volume III, paragraphs 693 and 704. In addition, Your Honours, beginning in early 1999, Pavkovic also brought VJ units into Kosovo in breach of the October Agreements in order to place the VJ in a position to engage in a campaign of violence when the NATO bombing began. And I refer Your Honours to Volume III, paragraphs 689 to 690, and paragraph 76. This conclusion, Your Honours, is borne-out by the evidence which the Trial Chamber relied upon in paragraph 689. First, in a media interview from 2000, Pavkovic stated: "We carried out a timely mobilisation, brought them to Kosovo in the greatest secrecy, distributed the war reserves, and blocked those forces without them even knowing it. The signal for a total blockade was the first rocket that came this way." And this is from P1319, page 17, and the reference to the forces being blocked is a reference to the KLA. Similarly, in a documentary from 2004, Pavkovic stated: "Our biggest strategic ruse was that we managed to bring in the new forces in front of Walker and that they did not know it, that we surrounded all of these groups, without Walker and themselves knowing it; their task was to surround them and destroy them if the aggression starts, if the first missile falls on our ground." And this is from P912, page 7, which is also -- which is cited at footnote 1689 of Volume III. And the reference, Your Honours, to Walker is a reference to William Walker, the head of the KVM mission that was responsible for ensuring the implementation of the October Agreements. And indeed, Your Honours, on the 23rd of March, 1999, the eve of the NATO bombing, Pavkovic put the VJ forces under his control in a position to carry out the expulsion campaign. That day, set out in paragraph 694 of Volume III, Pavkovic ordered that at the start of NATO strikes units were "to be immediately engaged against all enemy forces." And as Mr. Ackerman indicated this morning, this comes from Exhibit 4D103, and the Trial Chamber was right to rely on this exhibit as it did because when the NATO bombing began the next day, as described in vivid detail in Volume II of the judgement, so too did the systematic and organised campaign of terrorisation against the Kosovo Albanian population. And I refer Your Honours in this regard to Mr. Kremer's discussion of the pattern of crimes which appears at T 221 to T 232 of yesterday's transcript. From the nature of the campaign that was carried out, campaign of violence, we know what the objective of Pavkovic's military orders were. Throughout this expulsion campaign, Pavkovic maintained tight command and control over the VJ forces in Kosovo through his near constant presence on the ground. By his own admission, Pavkovic was in Kosovo more than 95 per cent of the time between March and June 1999. And this is at Volume III, paragraph 716. And if I could direct Your Honours' attention to the slide in front of you, as you'll see in the text highlighted in yellow, Lazarevic, who was the only accused to testify in this case, affirmed that during this conflict: "... not a single day went by without the army commander at the command post of the Pristina Corps." Of course, the army commander to whom Lazarevic refers is Pavkovic. And as Your Honours can see from the text highlighted in blue, Lazarevic added that it was rare for a commander of Pavkovic's position to locate himself as he did at the corps command. Having considered such evidence, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was right not to view Pavkovic as a mere conduit through whom orders were relayed as Pavkovic presents himself at paragraph 214 of his appeal brief. Instead, as the Chamber found at paragraph 782 of Volume III, through his presence on the ground, Pavkovic commanded the VJ troops who carried out the expulsion campaign. During this campaign, Pavkovic also worked closely with his fellow members of the Joint Command, Sainovic and Lukic, to co-ordinate the joint VJ-MUP operations. Pavkovic ensured that decisions adopted by the Joint Command were carried out by the VJ by giving his approval when Lazarevic prepared Joint Command decisions. And I refer Your Honours in this regard to trial judgement Volume III, paragraphs 462, 782, 1118; and Volume I, paragraphs 1037 to 1038, and 1151. As Your Honours will recall from Mr. Kremer's submission yesterday, several of the Joint Command decisions admitted into evidence identify forces engaging in operations in areas and on dates that correspond with crimes found proven by the Trial Chamber. And this is at Volume I, paragraph 1123; and Volume III, paragraph 695. The systematic way in which crimes were committed during the joint operations demonstrates that the objective of these operations was to expel the Kosovo Albanian population. As set out in Volume II of the judgement, when VJ and MUP forces were unleashed in joint operations, the result in most cases was devastation, as Kosovo Albanians villages were shelled, the homes of Kosovo Albanians were torched and looted, Kosovo Albanians were murdered, their religious structures were destroyed, and there were instances of sexual assault. Scores of Kosovo Albanians fled their homes from fear of the attacking forces or were forcefully rounded up and expelled. And again I refer Your Honours to Mr. Kremer's submission from yesterday concerning the pattern of crimes. As the Trial Chamber noted at paragraph 696 of Volume III, orders to displace Kosovo Albanians during such operations were generally never issued in writing, but instead passed down verbally. However, Your Honours will recall from Mr. Schneider's presentation the list of directions which Pavkovic issued to his subordinate commanders on the 7th of May, 1999. When Pavkovic issued these directions and in them instructed his subordinates to "ensure complete control of the territory and movement of Siptar civilians," the objective of the common purpose had almost been achieved and Pavkovic finally made explicit what had previously only been transmitted orally. Ultimately, Your Honours, over 700.000 Kosovo Albanians were forcibly displaced during the 1999 campaign in a little over two months. And now I would like to turn to the disarming of the Kosovo Albanian population. When sending forces into operations where the objective was to expel Kosovo Albanians, Pavkovic made use of the fact that, in 1998, he had rendered many Kosovo Albanians defenceless, by ordering and ensuring that they be disarmed. Pavkovic's involvement in the disarming process, which began in September 1998 and continued into October 1998, is addressed at paragraphs 668 to 669, and 57 to 58 of Volume III, and the evidence referred to therein. The Chamber found that the approach of disarming Kosovo Albanians "was designed to render the Kosovo Albanian population vulnerable to the forces of the FRY and Serbia." And this is at Volume III, paragraph 72. The ruthless efficiency with which Pavkovic and his fellow JCE members were able to implement the common purpose in the spring of 1999 demonstrates that the intended effect of the disarming process was achieved. I turn now, Your Honours, to the arming of the Kosovo Albanian population. Just as he had disarmed Kosovo Albanians in 1998, Pavkovic armed non-Albanians beginning in the summer of 1998. He then made use of these armed civilians during the operations that were carried out in 1999. Pavkovic's involvement in arming non-Albanians is discussed at paragraph 666 [sic] of Volume III. Now, this morning Mr. Ackerman said at page 11 of the transcript that: "You can go to every page of P1468, the Joint Command notes that are cited by the Trial Chamber, and you can see no indication of Pavkovic's support and leadership for the process of arming. It's mentioned on occasion by other persons, he's present there, but he says not a word." Well, I ask Your Honours to go to page 163 of the Joint Command notes, P1468, and this is from the 28th of October, 1998, and to read Pavkovic's comments, where he said: "We have to take into consideration how to use the armed population and how to involve it in the defence of communications." Your Honours, in his submissions this morning Mr. Ackerman cites to evidence which he says supports his argument but ignores relevant evidence relied upon by the Trial Chamber and this is but one example.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speaker to slow down for the purposes of interpretation. Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, the quote that I read out from page 163 of the Joint Command notes is from -- is referred to at paragraph 667 of Volume III and the transcript reads "666" right now so that needs to be corrected. Now, Your Honours, returning to those whom Pavkovic armed, those whom he armed were VJ reservists who were not actively engaged in war-time units. The MUP staff under Lukic similarly armed MUP reservists. Once they were armed, VJ and MUP reservists were sent back to their villages to form local defence units known as RPOs or reserve police detachments. Although the MUP maintained general command and control over these units, the VJ also played a role in commanding and controlling these units. And this is at Volume I, paragraph 778, 784 to 788. While most RPOs were disbanded when mobilisation commenced in March 1999, the Chamber found at paragraph 776 of Volume I that there still remained roughly 6.000 RPO members after mobilisation, and indeed Pavkovic engaged these armed non-Albanians in the VJ's operations in 1999, through orders which he issued and approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, counsel, if you also have trouble to speak slowly, you may also make a longer pause after each sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honour, I apologise for that. I will endeavour to speak slower through the remaining part of my submissions, and I thank Your Honours for the intervention. As I mentioned, Your Honour, Pavkovic engaged armed non-Albanians in the VJ's operations in 1999, through orders which he issued and approved. And the judgement cites for this are Volume III, paragraph 693; and Volume I, paragraphs 768, 780, 785, and 788. And when the expulsion campaign commenced, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found that in some instances armed non-Albanian civilians acted together with VJ and MUP soldiers in driving out Kosovo Albanians, including within Pristina and villages in the municipalities of Orahovac, Pec and Gnjilane. And I refer Your Honours to Volume II, paragraphs 48, 432, 888, and 944. Your Honours, this then brings me to the second aspect of Pavkovic's contribution. Once the criminal activity had begun, Pavkovic created and sustained an environment of impunity by taking wholly inadequate measures to prevent and punish crime and by concealing from his superiors within the VJ the full extent of what he knew was taking place on the ground. This enabled the criminal campaign in 1999 to continue. Although Pavkovic issued orders which called generally for crime prevention and respect for international law, these were token efforts which he knew would never halt or even stem the prevailing crime wave. And as one could expect, they had no impact. As the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 569 of Volume I, from its analysis of the relevant evidence, criminal offending was significantly underreported to the military justice system. The fact that Pavkovic was frequently in Kosovo between March and June 1999 and spent most of his time in Pristina where the Trial Chamber found that scores of Kosovo Albanians were expelled from the 24th of March, 1999, onwards, through operations that in the Chamber's words at paragraph 888 of Volume II "required significant planning and co-ordination," would have made it abundantly clear to Pavkovic's subordinates that he accepted, approved, and intended the forcible displacement campaign; that his calls for crime prevention and respect for international law were disingenuous; and that the violence targeted at the Kosovo Albanian population could be allowed to persist without repercussion. As far as other measures which Pavkovic took are concerned, the Trial Chamber reasonably considered them but concluded that they were not intended to limit criminal activity by the VJ. And I refer Your Honours to Volume III, paragraphs 721, 725, and 765. For example, Your Honours, in rejecting Pavkovic's dismissal of subordinate commanders as a genuine measure, the Trial Chamber referred to Pavkovic's admission that these commanders were removed because they failed to take "certain measures for protection and camouflaging of the units." This is at Volume III, paragraph 725. In addition, Mr. Ackerman this morning referred to Pavkovic's appointment of a commission concerning refugees in Istok in April 1999. Contrary to Mr. Ackerman's submission, the Trial Chamber did consider this evidence. It considered a duplicate of the exhibit which Mr. Ackerman referred to at transcript pages 44, 7 to 17. Having considered the evidence, the Chamber questioned the motivation behind the commission's report and its accuracy. And this is at Volume III, paragraph 721. Pavkovic's token efforts at suppressing crime were coupled with concealment. As Mr. Schneider alluded to in his presentation, Pavkovic kept information concerning the VJ's involvement in crime from his superiors within the General Staff. Even though meetings were organised by Pavkovic's superiors within the VJ on the 16th and the 17th of May, 1999, where the issue of serious crimes by the VJ, MUP, and paramilitary units was discussed, nothing was done as a result of these meetings because Milosevic was uninterested in resolving the issue of crime. And this is at Volume III, paragraphs 575 to 576, and 737 to 739. Thereafter, with Milosevic's stamp of approval, Pavkovic allowed the 3rd Army's practice of underreporting to continue through the end of the criminal campaign. And this is at Volume III, paragraph 752. In summary, then, Your Honours, Pavkovic was a critical member of the JCE who had been carefully positioned by Milosevic to ensure that the JCE succeeded. In the months leading up to the implementation of the common purpose, Pavkovic was actively involved in preparing for it. Once the common purpose was implemented, Pavkovic's conduct was critical to its success, as it was he who ensured the participation of the VJ. He not only planned, ordered, and supported VJ operations through which the crimes were committed; he also created and sustained an environment of impunity to ensure that nothing would get in the way of achieving the criminal objective. Pavkovic clearly made a significant contribution to the JCE and shared the intent of his fellow JCE members. We ask Your Honours that his appeal be dismissed and his sentence be adjusted in accordance with the Prosecution's appeal. Unless Your Honours have any further questions, those are our submissions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me there's no questions from the Bench. Does it mean that you're finished your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours. We have concluded our submissions. We have nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any reply from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a moment. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can't help but refer at the beginning to the chart that we were all handed at the beginning of the Prosecutor's presentation. And the thing I noted about it was that on all of the entries there are no citations to any evidence at all, no testimony, no documents, just sections of the judgement, as if the judgement is evidence. And the judgement is not evidence. Nothing in the judgement is evidence. It was argued a few moments ago in the first presentation that Pavkovic was aware of the Resolutions of the United Nations regarding what was happening on the ground in Kosovo. And if you get away from what's said in the judgement and go to what they are referring to in the evidence, it takes you to P1468 at page 161, where Pavkovic says this: "I ask that I be given in writing that the OSCE monitors can enter the barracks and count weapons. I believe that the principles as regulated in the Resolution of the UN should be respected." Period. There's nothing about Resolutions, as the Chamber says, and you cannot tell from this that Pavkovic was aware of the Resolutions of the UN dealing with what the UN said was going on on the ground. The Prosecution just told you a few moments ago and referred to some statements that Pavkovic made after the war to show you that he was aware that forces were being enhanced in early 1999 -- late 1998/early 1999. And we've never contended he was not aware. He was of course aware because he was there, he was a 3rd Army commander, he would know when forces had been assigned to his command. Our position is that he did not move forces into Kosovo in violation of the agreements; it was commanded down to him. This issue of arming, the Prosecutor just told you that I said there was nothing about Pavkovic with regard to arming in P1468 that showed his support and enthusiasm and leadership in that regard. And I stand by that proposition. What's on page 163 has nothing to do with support, leadership, enthusiasm, or anything else. He simply says: "We have to take into consideration how to use the armed population and how to involve it in the defence of communications." Now, understand we are at that point when the OSCE is coming in, they're -- the VJ has to remove a number of their forces, and the KLA is going to be strengthened in the process, and communications could become a problem. And so having these people that might be available to help with the communications issue could be important and ultimately -- he's just saying that that could be important. We keep hearing from the Prosecution about criminal activity that was underreported. And I don't know how you can say that activity is underreported if you don't know that it was happening in the first place. How could a person like Dimitrijevic, at his level, say that things were being underreported without knowing that things were happening that were being underreported. But there's no evidence at all that anything that had happened, any crimes that were occurring, were underreported. And I'll get to a little more detail on that in just a few minutes. Yesterday, in Volume III, paragraph 778, the Prosecution brought to your attention this language from the Trial Chamber with regard to Pavkovic: "His promotions to Commander of the 3rd Army and Chief of the General Staff were rewards from Milosevic to Pavkovic for his participation in the joint criminal enterprise." Now, if you look at Volume III, paragraph 778, you will find no footnote supporting that. It's not evidence. It's just a statement by the Trial Chamber, a supposition by the Trial Chamber. Document seizure is one of the significant events that is showing the existence of a plan, according to the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. And I was wondering yesterday evening what the evidence shows regarding the seizure of documents. I did as quick a survey as I could of the evidence, and I'm guessing - without knowing exactly - that there were around 10.000 Kosovo Albanians that had their documents seized. There were 750.000 refugees. That works out to about 1.33 per cent of the refugees having had their documents seized. For this to be a significant event, it would require proof of a more widespread seizure of documents than maybe 1.3 per cent. The OTP referred to Volume III, paragraph 34, and the quoted statement from the Trial Chamber of K89 that: "... 'not a single Albanian ear was to remain in Kosovo and that their identification papers were to be torn, so as to prevent them from coming back.'" What the Chamber left out and the Prosecution left out was the cross-examination of this witness. He was asked this question: "You mentioned ... the commander of your unit. You mentioned an order that he had issued. Am I correct when I tell you that" he "said that no ear of any terrorist should remain in combat?" The answer is: "Well, it's possible. I didn't understand whether he meant the ear of terrorists or any other persons." That's at transcript 9179, indicating this person really had no sense of what that statement really was. No reasonable Trial Chamber could conclude that he was talking about refugees instead of terrorists. I've discussed both K73 and K90 in my other presentation so I won't go there now. The Prosecution says yesterday that none of the Albanians who testified listed NATO bombing as a reason for their departure. Well, if I was in charge of the Prosecution in this case and I was concerned about that, then I get to choose the witnesses. And if some witness wants to say that NATO bombing was responsible for their departure, then I won't call that witness. I will call another Albanian witness that won't say that. The other thing we have to consider is that many of those people had to go back home after their testimony here, and that would have been an unpopular thing for them to have said back where they live. Who knows what would have happened to them. Volume III, paragraph 373, the Trial Chamber says this, and this was alluded to also yesterday: "According to Loncar, Sainovic instructed Lukic and Pavkovic to continue with the already established practice of informing him ... of important incidents first, and only then informing their ... superiors." That's the Trial Chamber language and they refer to Loncar's testimony at T 7652 to 54. Now, if you go there and look for that, you won't find it. What you will find is this. His answer was: "As stipulated, General Lukic was to report to him any police" -- to Sainovic "any police -- as regards any police matters, and General Pavkovic any army matters, or someone from their respective office." Nothing about informing him first and only then informing their superiors as if Sainovic was somehow deciding whether or not they should report certain things to their superiors. So it's a misleading interpretation by the Trial Chamber rather than an accurate account of what was said. Vasiljevic -- this whole business of Pavkovic being close to Milosevic and having a special relationship with Milosevic, and you keep hearing from the Prosecution that they got together and planned what was going on in Kosovo, there is zero evidence, zero, of them talking about anything to do with Kosovo. You're not going to find it. You will find one instance, one proven instance, of Pavkovic meeting with Milosevic and that's the one that was described by Vasiljevic in his testimony and that's at page 8669 of the transcript. And he talks about going to the White Palace with Ojdanic and Milosevic is leaving as they arrive. And then they go in and talk to Milosevic, and Ojdanic mentions that he saw Pavkovic leaving, and Milosevic says: "Well, you know, he was here not in an official capacity, he just dropped by." More important, this alleged meeting that had to do with planning in Kosovo happened in mid-June after the war was over. So it's useless as an exhibit for that proposition. Today at -- they talked about Volume III, 757, and I've got to see if I can find that now. At Volume III, 757, the Chamber says: "Pavkovic's response to the receipt of the indictment, that he was unable to take further measures against perpetrators of crimes in Kosovo ..." and then on about -- and they said that he said that it was found that he was unable to take measures against crimes in Kosovo because of the receipt of the indictment. Well, he never received an indictment. There's no evidence at all that he received any indictment. I don't know whether that's referring to that one statement by Krga in the meeting, saying that -- something about an indictment. I don't know what it's referring to, but I think it's a mistake. I think it's a typographical error by the Trial Chamber in the thing. I think they're talking about his receipt of the letter from Louise Arbour that was sent to him and that he responded to. And when he responded to it, what he said was - not that he couldn't continue to investigate crimes - what he said was -- she was asking to send representatives of ICTY to investigate in Kosovo. And he said in his report back to the joint -- to the General Staff, Supreme Command Staff: "I stress that I am not authorised to give this permission, but the authorised responsible organ of the federal government is ..." So that's all he was saying, not that he couldn't do anything. This afternoon you heard from the Prosecutor I think - and I may have misheard this, I think he said with regard to Pavkovic, his troops in the MUP would commit crimes, that he knew in 1998 his troops in the MUP would commit crimes. Well, Pavkovic never had any troops in the MUP and never had any control over the MUP and never ordered the MUP to do anything and couldn't. Gornje Obrinje was brought up and I need to talk about that. The Trial Chamber says at paragraph 774 with regard to Pavkovic: "He was informed of the violent crimes committed during joint VJ and MUP operations in Gornje Obrinje ... and of allegations that VJ and MUP were responsible for these crimes." And you go to the footnote and you start trying to find out where they come up with that information. The orders for and reports of the VJ actions in this area are found in 4DA17 - and these are new exhibits so they wouldn't have been able to the Chamber - 4DA17 of 9 September, 4DA19 of 22 September, 4DA20 of 23 September, 6D755 of 26 September, and 6D756 of 27 September. There followed after this action reports in the press and from humanitarian organisations regarding an alleged massacre of civilians in Gornje Obrinje on the 26th and 27th of September. In response to that, General Perisic sent a request for information to the 3rd Army; that's 4D403 of 2 October 1998. He asks for any information on the commission of a massacre, and if there was one, who committed it. The next day Samardzic sent the same request on down to the Pristina Corps to General Pavkovic; and that's 4D402. And on this same day, 3 October, Pavkovic sent an inquiry to units active in the area; and that's 4D199 of 3 October. He asked if they deviated in any way from the schedule of 26 and 27 September combat operations. And if they had any information of any massacre committed against civilians in the zones where their units were engaged, and if so, describe it and tell who participated in it. He requested a written report by 5 October. Numerous reports were received back. None had any information about a massacre; that's 4D387, 4D390, 4D391, 4D407, 4D389, 4D401. All said no massacre. The 125th Motorised Brigade reported the same thing with an exception. Colonel Zivanovic reported a conversation with the commander of a police unit in which he was told that a woman's body was found lying on top of what was presumed to be her three children in an improvised bunker. She was dead, probably hit by a bullet or shrapnel in an area where terrorists had opened fire. The children were alive. Thus, there was one civilian death reported to Pavkovic, likely by terrorist fire. This was certainly not evidence of any massacre of civilians by army or police forces. And that's P1011, pages 71 and 72. Pavkovic submitted his report to the 3rd Army on 5 October 1998. He reported that based on combat reports, regular intelligence reports, and written reports from all unit commanders, that's more sources than are in the evidence actually than just cited, there was no information about the alleged massacre against the civilian population in the village of Gornje Obrinje. He reported that the chief of security of the Pristina Corps had told him about a report that was submitted to the General Staff security department about an unchecked report that some members of MUP carrying out combat operations in the village had executed some persons taken into custody. He informed the -- he informed that this was not a massacre of the civilian population as reported in the media, but apparently had to do with some KLA persons who were arrested and then wound up being executed apparently. And that's P1440, 5 October 1998. But he reported this. Recall that the Trial Chamber made this finding. He was informed of the violent crimes committed during joint VJ and MUP operations in Gornje Obrinje and of allegations that the VJ and MUP were responsible for these crimes. No support for that. The Trial Chamber first cited to try to support it a Human Rights Watch report at P441. This report detailing alleged crimes at Gornje Obrinje contains nothing that indicates Pavkovic was informed of these crimes. It was issued in 1 February of 1999, that's what it was dated. P1011, pages 70 and 72, referred to previously, provide no information at all regarding these crimes. P1440, previously referred to, has nothing regarding the alleged Gornje Obrinje massacre. Pavkovic did learn from that report that Serbian police had reportedly executed some persons they'd taken into custody. He reported this information to Samardzic. The cited evidence does not support the conclusion that Pavkovic was informed of the violent crimes committed. He was informed of media reports of a massacre at that place but was not able to confirm it and certainly was not informed that VJ and MUP members were responsible for the crimes. The Trial Chamber then says: "His subsequent report sought to minimise the seriousness of the incident and omitted relevant" information "in his possession." The only thing that he had in his possession that was omitted from his report because it didn't relate to the question he was asked to report on was the dead woman that was found lying on top of three children who was not, according to what he was told, the victim of a crime. I want to now go to Volume III, paragraph -- Your Honour, may I ask how much time I'm going to have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you only have 12 minutes to finish your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I was wondering if I could have until 4.00 since we're scheduled for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, you could not benefit from the diligence of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll try anything, you know. In Volume III, paragraph 718, the Trial Chamber says that with respect to knowledge of crimes, Pavkovic was aware of the UN Security Council Resolutions -- well, I've already talked about that. I'll skip that. I want to go to the underreporting of crimes issue sort of quickly and briefly. It's just not the case that there was underreporting of crimes by Pavkovic and no evidence supports the contention. He could not have kept relevant crime information from the Supreme Command Staff had he wanted to. Daily reports were filed through the military court's chain of command. You can find that in 4D160. The 3rd Army legal affairs office would submit reports to the legal department of the Supreme Command Staff. As evidence of underreporting, in Volume III, 748, the Trial Chamber reported that the Pristina Corps report for 3 April 1999 contained reports regarding crimes such as murder and attempted murder, that's 5D84, and the report from the 3rd Army for that day omitted that information. And that's true. But if you look at 4D276, you see that the 3rd Army report was filed before the Pristina Corps report was received and said additional information will be forwarded as soon as received. So the 3rd Army report was filed before that information of the 3rd Army came. What is not clear and just assumed by the Trial Chamber is that the murders and attempted murders in the report were war crimes and not internal VJ-on-VJ or VJ-on-Serb civilian kinds of crimes, of which there were several. In paragraph 747, Volume III, the Trial Chamber refers to a report of 31 March 1999 from the 175th Infantry Brigade to the Pristina Corps. It reported that eight volunteers were arrested on suspicion of having committed the crime in Zegra of robbery and murder. This was not forwarded in the Pristina Corps report to the 3rd Army of 31 March or 1 April. 6D1135, 4D371. It was reported to the Pristina Corps prosecutor's office, however, on 31 March. 6D69, page 38. So what was supposed to happen did happen. The Prosecution contended today that the military court system was not working at capacity, that crimes were not being reported and not being processed, and that was partly the fault of Pavkovic. It's interesting to note that there is a document, Exhibit P953, that was not referred to by the Prosecution. This document reported that during the war, prosecutors received 18.541 criminal reports; that's 237 per day every day. They issued 6.708 indictments; that would be 86 per day every day. They issued 2.811 judgements; that's 36 per day every day. And there were 278 on-site investigations; that would be three and a half per day every day. Considering that they were operating under war-time conditions in Kosovo, with bombs falling daily, needing to move frequently, it looks like they stayed pretty busy. This is not on its face a system that appears to have been failing to punish violators. Your Honours, I'm going to finish now. It will take me a couple minutes. I recently noticed something from the Washington Post that I think is a lesson on how to look at a case such as this, written by a gentleman named Timothy Kudo who served as a captain in the Marine Corps in Afghanistan. And I simply do this like the Prosecution's chart, as something that might be of value in referencing what happened in this case. In the Perisic appeal that I read, the Trial Chamber in that case, different from the Trial Chamber in this case, emphasised that what was going on was a war. And many things happen in war, but it was a war. This Chamber didn't ever seem to appreciate what was going on here was really a war. Anyhow, Captain -- this captain from the Marine Corps who served in Afghanistan says this: While I was on patrol in Afghanistan in 2010, my squad saw a motorcycle racing toward us. The two riders did not respond to our shouts to stop and we began firing and killed them. The riders turned out to be unarmed civilians and one looked no older than 16. Every day I think about those people and others whose deaths I ordered. The images flow into my mind while I'm showering, walking down the street, or watching a movie. I'm haunted by the feeling that I'm no longer the good person that I once thought I was. The Afghan conflict, Kosovo conflict were similar with regard to the inability for the regular military forces to distinguish between legitimate fighters and civilians. That provokes the kind of mistakes that Captain Kudo spoke of eloquently. The Trial Chamber judgement is based on the proposition that Pavkovic as commander of the 3rd Army, following orders from his superior officers, failed to control the 150.000 persons under his command, that he was able to be everywhere all the time and in the minds of all his soldiers. That's an impossible burden to place on General Pavkovic. You've heard today and have read in our brief about the many efforts that he made to ensure that soldiers under his control abided by the rules of the law of war. He did more in that regard than anyone could have expected or demanded. The major Trial Chamber finding against him is that upon learning of the commission of crimes he continued to order VJ forces to support MUP forces in operations against KLA forces. Had he refused to do so, he would simply have been replaced. His refusal would not have changed the situation; it likely would have made it worse because he was working to protect the people. I was assigned to this case on 13 June 2005, almost eight years ago. I've carried the responsibility for General Pavkovic and his future in my hands for approximately 400 weeks. That's a significant part of my life as a lawyer. This Chamber is the Court of last resort for this General. When I finish today, I'll not likely be able to speak for him again. I need to trust that as he leaves my hands, he will be in good hands. I have to trust this Chamber to consider this case carefully and correctly, and I do. I do so knowing that you'll have in mind the words of Justice Jackson from nearly 70 years ago, when he said that in war crimes trials: "... any trials to which lawyers worthy of their calling lend themselves will be trials in fact, not merely trials in name, to ratify a predetermined result." Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a correction to the record from our submissions this morning. At transcript page 70, lines 15 through 16, the transcript reads: "Pavkovic was aware of the crimes of his subordinates in the MUP." What was intended to be said was that Pavkovic was aware of the crimes of his subordinates and the MUP, so I just want to make that correction for the record, Your Honours. We have nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that there's no questions from my colleagues, so that concludes the hearings for today. We adjourn these proceedings until tomorrow morning at 9.30 a.m.
